title: Lesson 22 · Bayesian regression and GLMs
text:
22.1 Bayesian logistic regression
The NO₂–asthma model of Lesson 8, with priors. Each 10 µg/m³ gets a prior on its log odds ratio; the adjustment variables get weakly informative priors too. With the full cohort, the prior barely matters. With a small sample, it does. Move the sample size and the prior, and compare the posterior with the frequentist estimate.


  Children in the analysis
  Prior for the log OR per 10 µg/m³Normal(0, 10²): vagueNormal(0, 0.5²): weakly informativeNormal(0, 0.1²): skeptical
  
  priorfrequentist estimate and 95% CIposterior






AStandard notation

\[Y_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_i), \qquad \mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i = \alpha + \beta\,\frac{\mathrm{NO}_{2,i}}{10} + \gamma^\top z_i\] \[\beta \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 0.5^2), \quad \gamma_k \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1), \quad \alpha \sim \mathrm{Normal}(-1.8, 1.5^2)\]

A Normal(0, 0.5²) prior on the log OR gives 95% prior probability to ORs between 0.38 and 2.7 per 10 µg/m³.




BModel list and R

fit <- brms::brm(
  asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green +
    parent_smoke + sex,
  family = bernoulli, data = cohort,
  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b,
                  coef = "Ino2_modeledD10"),
            prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),
            prior(normal(-1.8, 1.5),
                  class = Intercept)))



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): the same posterior by normal approximation, in base R






X <- model.matrix(~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green + parent_smoke + sex, data = cohort)
y <- cohort$asthma
prior_sd <- c(1.5, 0.5, rep(1, ncol(X) - 2)); prior_mean <- c(-1.8, rep(0, ncol(X) - 1))

neg_log_post <- function(b) {
  eta <- X %*% b
  -sum(y * eta - log1p(exp(eta))) + sum((b - prior_mean)^2 / (2 * prior_sd^2))
}
opt <- optim(rep(0, ncol(X)), neg_log_post, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
post_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(opt$hessian)))
exp(opt$par[2] + c(median = 0, low = -1.96, high = 1.96) * post_sd[2])   # OR per 10 ug/m3

#>    median       low      high 
#> 1.0533092 0.9474967 1.1709386











NoteR code (optional, not run when the site builds): the full brms model






fit <- brms::brm(
  asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green + parent_smoke + sex,
  family = bernoulli, data = cohort, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 22,
  prior = c(brms::prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b, coef = "Ino2_modeledD10"),
            brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),
            brms::prior(normal(-1.8, 1.5), class = Intercept)))
summary(fit)
draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit)
mean(exp(draws$b_Ino2_modeledD10) > 1)





Further reading: Gelman et al. (2008) propose weakly informative priors for logistic regression; Greenland (2007) on Bayesian regression in epidemiology; Bürkner (2017) describes brms.

title: Lesson 22 · Bayesian regression and GLMs
text:
22.2 Answering questions with posterior draws
Once you have posterior draws, every question is a computation on them. What is the probability that the odds ratio exceeds 1? That it exceeds 1.1? And, combining with Lesson 12, how many asthma cases per 1,000 children would a 10 µg/m³ reduction prevent? For that, g-computation is run once for every draw, giving a full posterior for the causal quantity.


  Threshold for "a meaningful effect" (OR per 10 µg/m³)
   use the true exposure (simulation only) instead of modeled NO₂
  
  






AStandard notation

\[P(OR > c \mid y) \approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_s 1\{e^{10\beta^{(s)}} > c\}\] \[\Delta^{(s)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i\Big[\pi_i^{(s)}(x_i) - \pi_i^{(s)}(x_i - 10)\Big]\]



BModel list and R

draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit)
mean(exp(draws$b_Ino2_modeledD10) > 1.1)
# g-computation on every draw
p_obs <- brms::posterior_epred(fit)
p_int <- brms::posterior_epred(fit,
  newdata = mutate(cohort, no2_modeled = no2_modeled - 10))
cases_prevented <- 1000 * rowMeans(p_obs - p_int)
quantile(cases_prevented, c(.025, .5, .975))



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Gelman, Hill, et al. (2020) on computing with posterior simulations; Kruschke (2015) on posterior probabilities of meaningful effects; Hernán and Robins (2020) on combining outcome models with standardization.

title: Lesson 22 · Bayesian regression and GLMs
text:
22.3 Posterior predictive checks
Does the model reproduce the data? A posterior predictive check simulates new datasets from the fitted model, one per posterior draw, and compares them with the real data. Here the data are daily visits by Old Town residents aged 65+. A Poisson model with only an intercept, a Poisson model with season and day of week, and a negative binomial model are checked against the observed distribution and its variance.


  ModelPoisson, intercept onlyPoisson + season + day of weeknegative binomial + season + day of week
  
  observed20 replicated datasets






AStandard notation

\[y^{\text{rep}(s)} \sim p(y \mid \theta^{(s)}), \qquad p_B = P\big(T(y^{\text{rep}}) \ge T(y) \mid y\big)\]

\(T\) = a test statistic, here the variance-to-mean ratio. \(p_B\) near 0 or 1 signals misfit.




BModel list and R

brms::pp_check(fit, ndraws = 20)
brms::pp_check(fit, type = "stat",
               stat = \(y) var(y) / mean(y))
# switch the likelihood:
brms::brm(..., family = negbinomial)








TipBayesian preview



Posterior predictive checks ask whether the model could have produced the data. They don’t choose between models. For that, Lesson 23 compares models by their out-of-sample predictive accuracy (LOO) and by Bayes factors, and shows when those two disagree.



Further reading: Gabry et al. (2019) on posterior predictive checks; Gelman et al. (2013) on model checking with replicated data; Ver Hoef and Boveng (2007) on choosing between quasi-Poisson and negative binomial models.

Key takeaways

Bayesian GLMs use the same model equations as Lesson 8, plus priors on the coefficients.
Priors on log odds ratios are easiest to set by thinking about plausible odds ratios; weakly informative priors rule out absurd values.
With much data the posterior matches the frequentist fit; with little data the prior matters, and its choice must be justified.
Posterior draws answer any question, including probabilities of meaningful effects and causal contrasts by g-computation.
Posterior predictive checks reveal misfit such as overdispersion; switch the likelihood when they fail.

section: 20.1 What does a prior say? Prior predictive checks
text:
20.1 What does a prior say? Prior predictive checks
A prior on α and β in log μ = α + β(T − 20) is hard to judge directly. Simulate from it instead: draw (α, β) from the prior, compute the curve of expected visits against temperature, and look. That is a prior predictive check. “Vague” priors with large standard deviations, often presented as letting the data speak, imply absurd numbers of visits.


  Prior SD of β (log scale, per °C)1 (vague)0.20.05 (weakly informative)0.01 (informative)
  Prior SD of α around log(8)10 (vague)20.5
  Draw again
  






AStandard notation

\[\alpha^{(s)} \sim p(\alpha), \quad \beta^{(s)} \sim p(\beta), \quad \tilde\mu^{(s)}(T) = e^{\alpha^{(s)} + \beta^{(s)}(T - 20)}\] \[\tilde y^{(s)} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\big(\tilde\mu^{(s)}(T)\big)\]



BModel list and R

a <- rnorm(100, log(8), 0.5)
b <- rnorm(100, 0, 0.05)
exp(a + b * (35 - 20))     # visits at 35°C

brms::brm(..., sample_prior = "only")








NoteR code (optional): a prior predictive check






set.seed(20)
prior_draws <- function(sd_a, sd_b, n = 1000)
  tibble(a = rnorm(n, log(8), sd_a), b = rnorm(n, 0, sd_b)) |>
  mutate(visits_35 = exp(a + b * 15))

bind_rows(vague = prior_draws(10, 1), weak = prior_draws(0.5, 0.05), .id = "prior") |>
  group_by(prior) |>
  summarise(median_visits_35C = median(visits_35),
            share_above_1000 = mean(visits_35 > 1000))

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   prior median_visits_35C share_above_1000
#>   <chr>             <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 vague              3.34            0.381
#> 2 weak               8.17            0






Further reading: Gabry et al. (2019) on prior predictive checks in the Bayesian workflow; Gelman et al. (2017) on understanding priors through the likelihood and data they imply; McElreath (2020) on simulating from priors.

section: 20.2 Eliciting a prior from subject knowledge
text:
20.2 Eliciting a prior from subject knowledge
Experts rarely think in log rate ratios, but they can usually say what range of effects they find plausible: “heat probably raises visits among older people by somewhere between 0% and 4% per degree.” That statement translates directly into a normal prior on β. Set the range, and check what the prior implies for a hot day.


  Lowest plausible effect (% per °C)
  Highest plausible effect (% per °C)
  






AStandard notation

\[\beta \sim \mathrm{Normal}(m, s^2), \quad m = \frac{\log(1 + L) + \log(1 + U)}{2}, \quad s = \frac{\log(1 + U) - \log(1 + L)}{2 \times 1.96}\]

\(L\) and \(U\): the lowest and highest plausible effects, read as a 95% prior range.




BModel list and R

L <- 0.00; U <- 0.04
m <- (log1p(L) + log1p(U)) / 2
s <- (log1p(U) - log1p(L)) / (2 * 1.96)
prior(normal(m, s), class = b)   # brms



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Spiegelhalter et al. (2004) on eliciting priors from clinical and epidemiological experts; Greenland (2006) on priors expressed as plausible ranges of relative risks; Greenland (2007) on informative priors in regression.

section: 20.3 How much does the prior matter?
text:
20.3 How much does the prior matter?
The same heat model from Lesson 19 is fitted under four priors, for increasing amounts of data. With little data, the priors give different answers. As data accumulate, the posteriors converge, unless the prior is so strong that it effectively ignores them. Reporting results under several priors is a sensitivity analysis.


Highlight: summer days of data







WarningCommon pitfall



Choosing the prior after seeing which one gives the preferred answer. Like choosing a spline’s flexibility by its result (Lesson 11), this invalidates the analysis. Specify the prior in advance, justify it, and report sensitivity to reasonable alternatives.



Further reading: Gelman et al. (2013) on sensitivity analysis; Spiegelhalter et al. (2004) on skeptical and enthusiastic priors as a community of opinions; Greenland (2006) on presenting results under several priors.

section: 20.4 Priors as penalties: shrinking and smoothing
text:
20.4 Priors as penalties: shrinking and smoothing
The posterior mode under a normal prior is the same as a penalized maximum likelihood estimate: the prior adds a penalty for coefficients far from its mean. This is the bridge between Bayesian priors and the penalized splines of Lesson 11. Here it is applied to the unconstrained distributed lag model of Lesson 16. An independent prior shrinks each lag coefficient toward zero; a random-walk prior shrinks neighboring lags toward each other, smoothing the curve.


  Independent normal (shrink to 0)Random walk (shrink toward smooth)
  Prior precision, log₁₀ λ
  






AStandard notation

\[\text{independent: } \beta_\ell \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1/\lambda)\] \[\text{random walk: } \beta_\ell - \beta_{\ell-1} \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1/\lambda)\] \[\log p(\beta \mid y) = \ell(\beta) - \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\,\beta^\top P \beta + \text{const}\]

\(P = I\) for the independent prior; \(P = D^\top D\), with \(D\) the first-difference matrix, for the random walk.




BModel list and R

b[1] ~ normal(0, 0.1)
b[l] ~ normal(b[l - 1], sigma_rw)    # l = 2..L
# mgcv: the same penalty, chosen by REML
mgcv::gam(visits ~ s(lag_matrix, by = temp_matrix,
                     bs = "ps"), ...)








TipBayesian preview



Here λ is fixed by hand. In a hierarchical model it becomes a parameter with its own prior, and the data decide how much to shrink or smooth, just as τ was estimated in Lesson 18. Lesson 24 makes this the central idea.



Further reading: Gelman et al. (2008) propose weakly informative default priors that act as gentle penalties; Eilers and Marx (1996) on difference penalties, the random-walk prior in frequentist form; Wood (2017) on the link between penalties and priors.

Key takeaways

Judge a prior by what it implies about data: simulate from it.

Plausible ranges from subject knowledge translate directly into normal priors on log relative risks.
The prior’s influence fades as data accumulate; report sensitivity to reasonable alternatives.
A normal prior acts as a penalty. Independent priors shrink toward zero; random-walk priors smooth.

title: Lesson 18 · Clustered data and mixed-effects models
text:
18.1 Clustering and the intraclass correlation
The 5,000 children attend 40 schools. If asthma risk varies between schools more than chance would explain, children in the same school are more alike than children from different schools. The intraclass correlation (ICC) measures this: the share of the variation that lies between clusters. Even a small ICC matters when clusters are large, through the design effect.







AStandard notation

\[\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_{ij} = \alpha + u_j, \qquad u_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau^2)\] \[ICC = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \pi^2/3}, \qquad \text{design effect} = 1 + (m - 1)\,ICC\]

\(i\) = child, \(j\) = school, \(m\) = average school size; \(\pi^2/3\) is the variance of the logistic distribution.




BModel list and R

asthma[i] ~ bernoulli(p[i])
logit(p[i]) = a + u[school[i]]
u[j] ~ normal(0, tau)

fit <- lme4::glmer(asthma ~ 1 + (1 | school),
                   family = binomial, data = cohort)
tau2 <- as.numeric(lme4::VarCorr(fit)$school)
tau2 / (tau2 + pi^2 / 3)       # ICC



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): random-intercept logistic model and ICC






fit0 <- lme4::glmer(asthma ~ 1 + (1 | school), family = binomial, data = cohort)
tau2 <- as.numeric(lme4::VarCorr(fit0)$school)
c(tau = sqrt(tau2), icc = tau2 / (tau2 + pi^2 / 3))

#>        tau        icc 
#> 0.32760873 0.03159296

fit1 <- lme4::glmer(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green + (1 | school),
                    family = binomial, data = cohort)
exp(lme4::fixef(fit1)[2])

#> I(no2_modeled/10) 
#>          1.034727






Further reading: Snijders and Bosker (2012) on the ICC and design effects; Gelman and Hill (2007) introduce multilevel models through examples; Bates et al. (2015) describe the lme4 software.

title: Lesson 18 · Clustered data and mixed-effects models
section: 18.2 No pooling, complete pooling and partial pooling
text:
18.2 No pooling, complete pooling and partial pooling
What is the asthma risk in each school? No pooling uses each school’s own data: unbiased but noisy for small schools. Complete pooling gives every school the overall risk: stable but wrong for schools that really differ. Partial pooling, what a random-effects model does, takes a weighted compromise. The weight depends on each school’s size and on how much schools truly differ (τ). Because the data are simulated, each school’s true risk is known, so you can see which approach gets closest.


  Between-school SD τ (logit scale)
  Estimate τ from the dataNo pooling (τ very large)Complete pooling (τ = 0)
  






AStandard notation

\[\hat\theta_j^{\text{pp}} = w_j\,\hat\theta_j + (1 - w_j)\,\hat\mu, \qquad w_j = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + s_j^2}\]

\(\hat\theta_j\): school \(j\)’s own log-odds, with standard error \(s_j\); \(\hat\mu\): overall log-odds.




BModel list and R

lme4::ranef(fit0)$school    # shrunken u_j
coef(fit0)$school |>         # alpha + u_j
  mutate(risk = plogis(`(Intercept)`))



Further reading: Efron and Morris (1977) explain why shrinkage improves many estimates at once; Gelman and Hill (2007) on no, complete and partial pooling; Snijders and Bosker (2012) on empirical Bayes estimates of random effects.

section: 18.3 Two-stage analysis: pooling district-specific heat effects
text:
18.3 Two-stage analysis: pooling district-specific heat effects
Multi-city temperature studies commonly use two stages: estimate the effect in each location separately, then combine the estimates in a random-effects meta-analysis. The meta-analysis gives a pooled effect, a measure of heterogeneity between locations, and improved location-specific estimates that borrow strength from the others. Here, each district’s heat effect for residents aged 65+ is estimated on summer days.

district's own estimateafter pooling (BLUP)pooled effect





AStandard notation

\[\hat\beta_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\beta_j, s_j^2), \qquad \beta_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \tau^2)\] \[Q = \sum_j \frac{(\hat\beta_j - \hat\beta_{\text{FE}})^2}{s_j^2}, \qquad I^2 = \max\!\left(0, \frac{Q - (J-1)}{Q}\right)\]



BModel list and R

# stage 1: one model per district (see 18.3 code)
# stage 2: random-effects meta-analysis
meta <- mixmeta::mixmeta(b ~ 1, S = se^2,
                         data = stage1,
                         method = "reml")
summary(meta)   # pooled effect, tau, I2
blup(meta)      # shrunken district effects



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): two-stage analysis of district heat effects






summer65 <- visits |>
  filter(month(date) %in% 6:8, age_group == "65+") |>
  mutate(heat = temp - 22)

stage1 <- summer65 |>
  group_by(district) |>
  group_modify(\(d, key) {
    f <- glm(visits ~ heat + dow, family = quasipoisson, data = d)
    tibble(b = coef(f)["heat"], se = sqrt(vcov(f)["heat", "heat"]))
  }) |>
  ungroup()

# DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling, written out
w  <- 1 / stage1$se^2
fe <- sum(w * stage1$b) / sum(w)
Q  <- sum(w * (stage1$b - fe)^2)
tau2 <- max(0, (Q - (nrow(stage1) - 1)) / (sum(w) - sum(w^2) / sum(w)))
wr <- 1 / (stage1$se^2 + tau2)
c(pooled_pct_per_degC = 100 * (exp(sum(wr * stage1$b) / sum(wr)) - 1),
  tau = sqrt(tau2), I2 = max(0, (Q - (nrow(stage1) - 1)) / Q))

#> pooled_pct_per_degC                 tau                  I2 
#>            1.062927            0.000000            0.000000






Further reading: DerSimonian and Laird (1986) introduced the random-effects estimator used here; Higgins and Thompson (2002) defined I²; Gasparrini et al. (2012) extended two-stage pooling to whole exposure–response curves, as used in multi-city DLNM studies.

title: Lesson 18 · Clustered data and mixed-effects models
section: 18.4 Standard errors when observations are clustered
text:
18.4 Standard errors when observations are clustered
Ignoring clustering gives standard errors that are too small, because correlated observations carry less information than independent ones. The problem is worst for cluster-level exposures, which vary only between clusters: district traffic, for instance, takes just 12 values. Cluster-robust standard errors, or random-effects models, correct this.


  ExposureSES score (varies between children)district traffic (varies only between districts)modeled NO₂ (varies mostly between districts)
  Clustersschools (40)districts (12)
  






AStandard notation

\[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\text{CR}}(\hat\beta) = I^{-1}\Big(\sum_{c} U_c U_c^\top\Big) I^{-1}, \qquad U_c = \sum_{i \in c} x_i\,(y_i - \hat\pi_i)\]

\(I\) = information matrix from the ordinary model; \(U_c\) = score contribution of cluster \(c\).




BModel list and R

fit <- glm(asthma ~ traffic, family = binomial,
           data = cohort_d)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))                    # naive
sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovCL(fit,
          cluster = ~ district)))        # robust








TipBayesian preview



A random effect is a prior whose spread τ is estimated from the data. Bayesian hierarchical models make this explicit: they put a prior on τ itself and carry its uncertainty into every group estimate. With few groups, such as 12 districts, that uncertainty matters, and frequentist estimates of τ are often unstable. Lesson 24 develops this.



Further reading: Gelman and Hill (2007) on the consequences of ignoring clustering; Snijders and Bosker (2012) on cluster-level predictors and design effects; Fox (2016) on sandwich estimators.

title: Lesson 16 · Distributed lag and distributed lag non-linear models
section: 16.1 Lagged effects and the distributed lag model
text:
16.1 Lagged effects and the distributed lag model
A hot day can raise visits on the same day, the next day and the day after. A distributed lag model includes the exposure on each of the previous L days, each with its own coefficient. Here the exposure is “degrees above 20°C” (heat only). Unconstrained, the lag coefficients are noisy, because temperatures on neighboring days are highly correlated. Constraining the lag curve to a smooth shape stabilizes it. Watch for negative coefficients a few days after a hot spell: that is harvesting.


  Maximum lag (days)
  Unconstrained: one coefficient per lagConstrained: smooth lag curve
  






AStandard notation

\[\log\mu_t = \alpha + \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\beta_\ell\, h_{t-\ell} + s(t) + \gamma^\top \mathrm{dow}_t, \qquad h_t = \max(0, T_t - 20)\] \[\text{constrained: } \beta_\ell = \sum_k \theta_k\, c_k(\ell), \qquad \text{cumulative} = \sum_\ell \beta_\ell\]



BModel list and R

cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(pmax(city_daily$temp - 20, 0),
        lag = 10,
        argvar = list(fun = "lin"),
        arglag = list(fun = "ns", df = 4))
fit <- glm(visits ~ cb + splines::ns(t, df = 35) + dow,
           family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)



Further reading: Schwartz (2000) on distributed lag models and harvesting; Armstrong (2006) on lagged temperature effects; Gasparrini et al. (2010) on constraining lag structures.

title: Lesson 16 · Distributed lag and distributed lag non-linear models
text:
16.2 The DLNM: an exposure–lag–response surface
Temperature effects are both nonlinear (a U shape) and lagged. A DLNM handles both at once with a cross-basis: a spline in temperature multiplied by a spline in lag. The result is a surface: the relative risk at every combination of temperature and lag, relative to a reference temperature. Read it through slices: pick a temperature to see how its effect unfolds over the following days, or pick a lag to see the exposure–response at that delay.


  
  lower risk than at the referencehigher risk
  Temperature slice (°C)
  Lag slice (days)






AStandard notation

\[\log\mu_t = \alpha + \sum_{j}\sum_{k}\eta_{jk}\, w_{t,jk} + s(t) + \gamma^\top \mathrm{dow}_t\] \[w_{t,jk} = \sum_{\ell=0}^{L} b_j(T_{t-\ell})\, c_k(\ell)\]

\(b_j\): spline basis in temperature; \(c_k\): spline basis in lag; the \(\eta_{jk}\) define the whole surface.




BModel list and R

cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(city_daily$temp, lag = 21,
  argvar = list(fun = "ns", knots = quantile(
    city_daily$temp, c(.10, .50, .90))),
  arglag = list(fun = "ns",
    knots = dlnm::logknots(21, 3)))
fit <- glm(visits ~ cb + splines::ns(t, df = 35) +
             dow, family = quasipoisson,
           data = city_daily)

section: 16.3 The cumulative curve and the minimum morbidity temperature
text:
16.3 The cumulative curve and the minimum morbidity temperature
Summing the surface over all lags gives the cumulative exposure–response curve: the total effect of a day’s temperature over the following three weeks. Its lowest point is the minimum morbidity temperature (MMT), the usual reference. The MMT is itself an estimate, and often an uncertain one. Simulating from the fitted coefficients shows how uncertain, and what that uncertainty does to the relative risks reported against it.


   show the true curve (simulation)
  Simulate MMT uncertainty (500 draws)
  
  






AStandard notation

\[\log RR_{\text{cum}}(x) = \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{j,k}\eta_{jk}\,\big[b_j(x) - b_j(x_{\text{ref}})\big]\, c_k(\ell)\] \[\mathrm{MMT} = \arg\min_x \log RR_{\text{cum}}(x)\]



BModel list and R

pred <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = 20,
                        by = 0.1)
mmt <- pred$predvar[which.min(pred$allRRfit)]
pred2 <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = mmt,
                         at = quantile(city_daily$temp,
                                       c(.01, .99)))
pred2$allRRfit; pred2$allRRlow; pred2$allRRhigh



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Reporting relative risks against the MMT as if the MMT were known. Conventional intervals shrink to zero width at the reference, hiding its uncertainty. Report an interval for the MMT itself, obtained by simulation or bootstrap.








NoteR code (optional): a DLNM for daily visits






city_daily <- visits |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(visits = sum(visits), temp = first(temp_city), dow = first(dow), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(t = row_number())

cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(city_daily$temp, lag = 21,
        argvar = list(fun = "ns", knots = quantile(city_daily$temp, c(.10, .50, .90))),
        arglag = list(fun = "ns", knots = dlnm::logknots(21, 3)))
fit <- glm(visits ~ cb + splines::ns(t, df = 35) + dow, family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)

pred <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = 20, by = 0.1)
mmt <- pred$predvar[which.min(pred$allRRfit)]
pred <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = mmt, by = 0.1)
plot(pred, "overall", xlab = "Temperature (°C)", ylab = "Cumulative RR (lags 0-21)")







mmt

#> [1] 19.4






Further reading: Tobías et al. (2017) on estimating uncertainty in the minimum mortality temperature; Gasparrini et al. (2015) report cumulative temperature–mortality curves in 384 locations; Gasparrini (2011) on predicting from a DLNM.

title: Lesson 16 · Distributed lag and distributed lag non-linear models
text:
16.4 Heat- and cold-attributable visits
From the cumulative curve, each day’s visits can be split into those attributable to that day’s temperature (relative to the MMT) and the rest. Summed over the period, this gives the attributable fraction for heat (days warmer than the MMT) and cold (days colder). Uncertainty is again obtained by simulating from the coefficients.


  Compute attributable visits (500 simulations)
  






AStandard notation

\[AF_t = 1 - \exp\{-\log RR_{\text{cum}}(T_t)\}, \qquad AN = \sum_t y_t\, AF_t\] \[AF_{\text{heat}} = \frac{\sum_{t: T_t > \mathrm{MMT}} y_t\, AF_t}{\sum_t y_t}\]



BModel list and R

# attrdl() from the dlnm tutorial code
# (Gasparrini & Leone 2014):
# attrdl(city_daily$temp, cb, city_daily$visits,
#        fit, type = "af", cen = mmt,
#        range = c(mmt, 100), sim = TRUE)



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



A Bayesian DLNM gives the lag curve a smoothing prior instead of a fixed number of spline knots, and computes the MMT and attributable fractions on every posterior draw, so their uncertainty comes for free. Lesson 25 builds a district-level Bayesian DLNM in which each district’s curve borrows strength from its neighbors.



Further reading: Gasparrini and Leone (2014) define attributable risk from distributed lag models; Gasparrini et al. (2015) apply it across countries; Rockhill et al. (1998) on interpreting attributable fractions.

title: Lesson 14 · Measuring disease burden
section: 14.1 Attributable fractions for a binary exposure
text:
14.1 Attributable fractions for a binary exposure
The population attributable fraction (PAF) is the share of cases in a population that would not occur without the exposure. It combines how common the exposure is with how much it raises risk. Levin’s formula uses the exposure prevalence and the risk ratio; it is valid only with an unconfounded risk ratio. With confounding, Miettinen’s formula, which uses the proportion of cases exposed and an adjusted risk ratio, remains valid.


  Prevalence of exposure
  Risk ratio
  Use the cohort: NO₂ ≥ 30 µg/m³
  






AStandard notation

\[PAF_{\text{Levin}} = \frac{p_e\,(RR - 1)}{1 + p_e\,(RR - 1)}\] \[PAF_{\text{Miettinen}} = p_c\,\frac{RR_{\text{adj}} - 1}{RR_{\text{adj}}}\]

\(p_e\) = proportion of the population exposed; \(p_c\) = proportion of cases exposed.




BModel list and R

d  <- cohort |> mutate(high = no2_true >= 30)
pe <- mean(d$high)
pc <- mean(d$high[d$asthma == 1])
paf_levin <- pe * (rr - 1) / (1 + pe * (rr - 1))
paf_miet  <- pc * (rr_adj - 1) / rr_adj



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Levin (1953) proposed the attributable fraction; Miettinen (1974) gave the formula valid under confounding; Rockhill et al. (1998) review the use and misuse of PAFs; Greenland and Robins (1988) on what attributable fractions do and don’t measure.

title: Lesson 14 · Measuring disease burden
section: 14.2 Continuous exposures and the counterfactual level
text:
14.2 Continuous exposures and the counterfactual level
NO₂ isn’t present or absent: every child is exposed to some level. The burden is computed against a counterfactual exposure, often called the theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL). Children above it contribute excess risk; children at or below it contribute none. The choice of counterfactual can matter more than any statistical decision. Move it, and compare zero, the WHO 2021 guideline of 10 µg/m³, and the former guideline of 40.


  Counterfactual NO₂ (µg/m³)
  Exposure–response fromthe true effect (simulation: OR 1.15 per 10)the naive estimate with modeled NO₂the regression-calibrated estimate
  






AStandard notation

\[PAF = 1 - \frac{E\big[\,P(Y = 1 \mid X = \min(x_i, x^*), Z = z_i)\,\big]}{E\big[\,P(Y = 1 \mid X = x_i, Z = z_i)\,\big]}\] \[AN = PAF \times D\]

\(x^*\) = counterfactual exposure; \(D\) = total cases. This is g-computation (Lesson 12) with the intervention “cap NO₂ at \(x^*\)”.




BModel list and R

fit <- glm(asthma ~ no2_true + ses + green,
           family = binomial, data = cohort)
r_obs <- mean(predict(fit, type = "response"))
r_cf  <- mean(predict(fit,
  mutate(cohort, no2_true = pmin(no2_true, 10)),
  type = "response"))
paf <- 1 - r_cf / r_obs



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Reporting a burden estimate without stating the counterfactual exposure, or comparing burden estimates that used different ones. A PAF relative to zero NO₂ and a PAF relative to 40 µg/m³ answer different questions, and can differ several-fold.








NoteR code (optional): PAF and attributable cases for several counterfactuals






fit <- glm(asthma ~ no2_true + ses + green, family = binomial, data = cohort)
r_obs <- mean(predict(fit, type = "response"))
paf_at <- function(x_star) {
  r_cf <- mean(predict(fit, mutate(cohort, no2_true = pmin(no2_true, x_star)), type = "response"))
  1 - r_cf / r_obs
}
tibble(counterfactual = c(0, 10, 20, 40)) |>
  mutate(paf = map_dbl(counterfactual, paf_at),
         cases_per_10000 = 10000 * r_obs * paf)

#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   counterfactual     paf cases_per_10000
#>            <dbl>   <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1              0 0.306             420. 
#> 2             10 0.215             295. 
#> 3             20 0.122             168. 
#> 4             40 0.00803            11.0






Further reading: Achakulwisut et al. (2019) estimate the global burden of paediatric asthma attributable to NO₂; Khreis et al. (2017) meta-analyze traffic pollution and childhood asthma incidence; World Health Organization (2021) set the current NO₂ guideline; Ezzati et al. (2002) describe the comparative risk assessment framework.

title: Lesson 14 · Measuring disease burden
text:
14.3 From cases to DALYs
Attributable cases count events; disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) measure lost healthy life, so that burdens from different diseases can be compared. DALYs add years of life lost (YLL) to early death and years lived with disability (YLD), weighted by the severity of the condition. For childhood asthma, YLD dominate. The inputs below are illustrative; real analyses take disability weights and durations from sources such as the Global Burden of Disease study.


  Attributable cases per year (from 14.2)
  Average duration of asthma (years)
  Disability weight
  Attributable deaths per year
  Remaining life expectancy at death
  Take cases from 14.2
  






AStandard notation

\[DALY = YLL + YLD\] \[YLL = \sum_a D_a\,L_a, \qquad YLD = I \times DW \times L_{\text{dur}}\]

Incidence-based YLD: new cases \(I\), disability weight \(DW\), average duration \(L_{\text{dur}}\).




BModel list and R

yld  <- cases * dw * duration
yll  <- deaths * life_expectancy
daly <- yll + yld



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Murray (1994) set out the technical basis of DALYs; GBD 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators (2020) report risk-factor burdens with current methods; Ezzati et al. (2002) on combining burden across risk factors.

title: Lesson 14 · Measuring disease burden
text:
14.4 Propagating uncertainty
A burden estimate inherits uncertainty from every input: the relative risk, the exposure distribution, the baseline risk. Plugging the confidence limits of the relative risk into the formula gives a crude range. Monte Carlo simulation does better: draw each input from a distribution expressing its uncertainty, compute the burden for each draw, and summarize the resulting distribution.


   uncertainty in the exposure–response coefficient
   uncertainty in the baseline risk
   uncertainty in duration (5 to 15 years) and disability weight (0.03 to 0.08)
  Run 4,000 simulations
  









TipBayesian preview



Monte Carlo propagation is the frequentist analyst borrowing a Bayesian idea: treating inputs as uncertain quantities with distributions. In a fully Bayesian analysis, the burden is a derived quantity computed on every posterior draw, so all uncertainties, and their correlations, flow through automatically. The capstone (Lesson 25) computes heat-attributable visits and DALYs this way.



Further reading: GBD 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators (2020) describe uncertainty intervals from repeated draws; Achakulwisut et al. (2019) propagate uncertainty in exposure–response and incidence; Greenland and Robins (1988) on why attributable fractions for several risk factors needn’t sum to 100%.

title: Lesson 12 · Causal inference: from association to effect
section: 12.1 Potential outcomes: two worlds, one observed
text:
12.1 Potential outcomes: two worlds, one observed
Imagine two worlds. In one, every child lives with the NO₂ they actually had. In the other, an intervention has reduced every child’s NO₂ by Δ µg/m³. Each child has a potential outcome in each world. The causal effect compares the two worlds for the same children. Real data show only the first world. Here, because the data are simulated, both can be shown.


  Reduction in NO₂, Δ (µg/m³)
  
  asthma in both worldsasthma prevented by the reductionno asthma in either world






AStandard notation

\[Y_i^{x}: \text{ outcome of child } i \text{ if exposure were set to } x\] \[RR_{\text{causal}} = \frac{E[Y^{X-\Delta}]}{E[Y^{X}]}, \qquad RD_{\text{causal}} = E[Y^{X-\Delta}] - E[Y^{X}]\]

Only \(Y_i^{X_i}\), the outcome under the exposure actually received, is ever observed (consistency).




BModel list and R

# the causal question, written as a contrast:
# E[asthma | everyone's NO2 lowered by 10]
#   vs E[asthma | NO2 as observed]
# Identification needs:
#   exchangeability given (SES, green)
#   positivity: every child could have had
#     NO2 10 µg/m3 lower
#   consistency: "lowering NO2" is well defined



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Hernán and Robins (2020) develop causal inference from potential outcomes; Hernán and Robins (2016) on framing observational analyses as emulations of a target trial; Greenland et al. (1999) on the formal definition of confounding.

title: Lesson 12 · Causal inference: from association to effect
section: 12.2 G-computation: estimating the two worlds from data
text:
12.2 G-computation: estimating the two worlds from data
G-computation, also called standardization, estimates each world with an outcome model. Fit a regression of asthma on NO₂ and confounders; predict every child’s risk with their own NO₂, and again with NO₂ lowered by Δ; average each set of predictions; compare. The result is a marginal effect for this population, the quantity the policy question asks for, and it can be compared directly with the truth from 12.1.


  Reduction Δ (µg/m³)
  Outcome model adjusts fornothing (crude)SES onlySES and green space (the DAG's minimal set)SES, green, parental smoking, sex
  






AStandard notation

\[\widehat{E}[Y^{x}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{P}(Y = 1 \mid X = x_i,\ Z = z_i)\]

Evaluated once with each child’s own \(x_i\), once with \(x_i - \Delta\); \(Z\) = confounders.




BModel list and R

fit <- glm(asthma ~ no2_true + ses + green,
           family = binomial, data = cohort)
r1 <- mean(predict(fit, cohort, type = "response"))
r0 <- mean(predict(fit,
        mutate(cohort, no2_true = no2_true - 10),
        type = "response"))
c(rr = r0 / r1, rd = r0 - r1)



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): g-computation with a bootstrap confidence interval






gcomp <- function(d, delta = 10) {
  fit <- glm(asthma ~ no2_true + ses + green, family = binomial, data = d)
  r_obs <- mean(predict(fit, d, type = "response"))
  r_int <- mean(predict(fit, mutate(d, no2_true = no2_true - delta), type = "response"))
  c(rr = r_int / r_obs, cases_prevented_per_1000 = 1000 * (r_obs - r_int))
}
gcomp(cohort)

#>                       rr cases_prevented_per_1000 
#>                0.8880198               15.3636874

set.seed(12)
boot <- map(1:200, \(b) as_tibble_row(gcomp(slice_sample(cohort, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)))) |>
  bind_rows()
apply(boot, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))

#>              rr cases_prevented_per_1000
#> 2.5%  0.7689192                0.4975408
#> 97.5% 0.9963491               31.5739105











WarningCommon pitfall



Reading an adjusted odds ratio as a population effect. The aOR is conditional on the covariates, and because odds ratios are non-collapsible it differs from the marginal OR even without confounding. G-computation turns a model into the marginal risk ratio or risk difference the question asks for.



Further reading: Snowden et al. (2011) demonstrate g-computation step by step; Hernán and Robins (2020) treat standardization and the g-formula; Keiding and Clayton (2014) link it to classical standardization.

title: Lesson 12 · Causal inference: from association to effect
section: 12.3 Propensity scores and inverse probability weighting
text:
12.3 Propensity scores and inverse probability weighting
A second route models the exposure instead of the outcome. The propensity score is each child’s probability of high NO₂ (here ≥ 30 µg/m³) given the confounders. Weighting each child by the inverse probability of the exposure they actually had creates a pseudo-population in which the confounders are balanced between exposed and unexposed. Check the overlap and the balance, and see what happens if the propensity model includes a variable that predicts exposure strongly but isn’t a confounder.


  Propensity model for high NO₂ (≥ 30 µg/m³):
   SES  green space  district traffic (not a confounder)
  Trim propensity scores outside
  
  high NO₂lower NO₂






AStandard notation

\[e(z) = P(A = 1 \mid Z = z), \qquad w_i = \frac{A_i}{e(z_i)} + \frac{1 - A_i}{1 - e(z_i)}\] \[\widehat{E}[Y^{a}] = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, 1\{A_i = a\}\, Y_i}{\sum_i w_i\, 1\{A_i = a\}}\]



BModel list and R

d <- cohort |> mutate(high = no2_true >= 30)
ps <- glm(high ~ ses + green, family = binomial,
          data = d) |> fitted()
d$w <- ifelse(d$high, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps))
with(d, weighted.mean(asthma[high], w[high]) /
        weighted.mean(asthma[!high], w[!high]))



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): weights, balance and the weighted risk ratio






d <- cohort |> mutate(high = no2_true >= 30)
ps_fit <- glm(high ~ ses + green, family = binomial, data = d)
d <- d |> mutate(ps = fitted(ps_fit), w = if_else(high, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps)))

smd <- function(x, g, w) {
  m1 <- weighted.mean(x[g], w[g]); m0 <- weighted.mean(x[!g], w[!g])
  (m1 - m0) / sqrt((var(x[g]) + var(x[!g])) / 2)
}
tibble(variable = c("ses", "green"),
       before = c(smd(d$ses, d$high, rep(1, nrow(d))), smd(d$green, d$high, rep(1, nrow(d)))),
       after  = c(smd(d$ses, d$high, d$w), smd(d$green, d$high, d$w)))

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   variable before   after
#>   <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 ses      -0.417 -0.0753
#> 2 green    -1.98  -0.329

with(d, weighted.mean(asthma[high], w[high]) / weighted.mean(asthma[!high], w[!high]))

#> [1] 1.219046

summary(d$w)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.000   1.029   1.131   1.892   1.515  93.259






Further reading: Austin (2011) introduces propensity score methods; Cole and Hernán (2008) on constructing and checking inverse probability weights; Westreich and Cole (2010) on positivity violations in practice.

title: Lesson 12 · Causal inference: from association to effect
section: 12.4 How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be?
text:
12.4 How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be?
Every observational estimate assumes no unmeasured confounding. The E-value asks: how strongly would an unmeasured confounder need to be associated with both the exposure and the outcome (as risk ratios) to fully explain away the observed association? Here, pretend green space had not been measured, and see how the estimate and its E-value compare.


  Observed risk ratio
  Lower 95% confidence limit
  Use the cohort estimate (SES + green)Use the estimate without green space
  






AStandard notation

\[E = RR + \sqrt{RR\,(RR - 1)}\] \[\text{explains away if } \frac{RR_{EU}\, RR_{UD}}{RR_{EU} + RR_{UD} - 1} \ge RR\]

\(RR_{EU}\): confounder–exposure association; \(RR_{UD}\): confounder–outcome association.




BModel list and R

e_value <- function(rr) rr + sqrt(rr * (rr - 1))
e_value(1.12)   # point estimate
e_value(1.01)   # lower confidence limit
# or: EValue::evalues.RR(1.12, lo = 1.01)



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



In a Bayesian analysis, g-computation is done on every posterior draw of the outcome model, giving a full posterior for the causal risk ratio. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding can be expressed as a prior on the bias parameters, so that uncertainty about the confounder enters the final interval (probabilistic bias analysis, Lesson 13).



Further reading: VanderWeele and Ding (2017) introduced the E-value; Fox et al. (2021) on quantitative bias analysis more generally; Hernán and Robins (2020) on the role of each identification assumption.

Key takeaways

A causal effect compares potential outcomes for the same population under two well-defined interventions. Only one is ever observed.
Identifying it from data needs exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding), positivity and consistency.
G-computation predicts both worlds from an outcome model and averages, giving marginal risk ratios and risk differences.
Inverse probability weighting balances confounders by weighting; check balance, overlap and extreme weights.
Don’t put non-confounders that strongly predict exposure into a propensity model: they worsen positivity and precision.
E-values express how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain an association away.

title: Lesson 10 · Model checking, comparison and selection
section: 10.1 Building and checking a model step by step
text:
10.1 Building and checking a model step by step
Here is the daily count of emergency visits in the whole city, modeled with Poisson regression. Add terms one at a time and watch three diagnostics: the residuals over time (patterns mean something is missing), their autocorrelation (today’s residual predicting tomorrow’s), and the dispersion. The table compares each term’s contribution with a likelihood ratio test.


  Terms in the model of daily city-wide visits:
   day of week
   season (annual cycle)
   long-term trend
   temperature (spline)
   PM2.5
  
  






AStandard notation

\[LR = 2\,(\ell_1 - \ell_0) \sim \chi^2_{k} \ \text{under } H_0\] \[AIC = -2\ell + 2p, \qquad QAIC = -\frac{2\ell}{\hat\phi} + 2p\]

\(k\) = parameters added; \(p\) = parameters in the model. For quasi-Poisson models, the LR statistic is divided by \(\hat\phi\).




BModel list and R

m0 <- glm(visits ~ dow, family = quasipoisson,
          data = city_daily)
m1 <- update(m0, . ~ . + sin(2*pi*doy/365.25) +
               cos(2*pi*doy/365.25))
anova(m0, m1, test = "F")   # quasi-Poisson
acf(residuals(m1, type = "pearson"))



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): building the model and checking residual autocorrelation






city_daily <- visits |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(visits = sum(visits), temp = first(temp_city), pm25 = first(pm25),
            dow = first(dow), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(doy = yday(date), t = as.numeric(date - min(date)))

m_dow  <- glm(visits ~ dow, family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)
m_full <- glm(visits ~ dow + sin(2*pi*doy/365.25) + cos(2*pi*doy/365.25) + t +
                splines::ns(temp, df = 4) + pm25, family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)
anova(m_dow, m_full, test = "F")

#> Analysis of Deviance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: visits ~ dow
#> Model 2: visits ~ dow + sin(2 * pi * doy/365.25) + cos(2 * pi * doy/365.25) + 
#>     t + splines::ns(temp, df = 4) + pm25
#>   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance      F    Pr(>F)    
#> 1      1820    22734.6                                 
#> 2      1812     3158.9  8    19576 1401.5 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

summary(m_full)$dispersion

#> [1] 1.746014

text:
10.2 Overfitting and cross-validation
A more flexible model always fits the data it was estimated on better. The question is whether it predicts new data better. Here a polynomial in temperature is fitted to a small training sample of days, and its predictions are scored on all the other days. Increase the degree: the training error keeps falling, the test error eventually rises. That gap is overfitting. Cross-validation estimates the test error using only the training data.

  Training days
  New training sample

title: Lesson 10 · Model checking, comparison and selection
text:
10.3 Influential observations
Least squares squares the residuals, so a single unusual point can pull a line strongly. Influence combines an unusual outcome (a large residual) with an unusual predictor value (high leverage). Move the extra child around and watch the slope and Cook’s distance, which measures how much the fitted values change when that point is removed.


  Extra child's green space
  Extra child's NO₂
  
  line without the extra childline with the extra child

title: Lesson 10 · Model checking, comparison and selection
text:
10.4 Why stepwise selection misleads
Choosing variables because they are “significant” in the same data used to report them makes those p-values meaningless. Here, 20 candidate predictors of asthma are pure noise. A screening rule keeps those with p < 0.05. Run it many times: noise variables are selected regularly, and every selected one comes with a “significant” p-value, by construction.


  Noise candidates
  Children per study
  Run 500 studies
  









WarningCommon pitfall



Selecting confounders by stepwise regression or by “a change in estimate of more than 10%”, then reporting the final model’s confidence intervals as if it had been chosen in advance. Confounders should be chosen from causal knowledge (a DAG, Lesson 9), and the model fixed before looking at the outcome.








TipBayesian preview



Bayesian analysis compares models in two ways: by Bayes factors, which ask which model predicted the data better before seeing it, and by leave-one-out cross-validation, the Bayesian counterpart of AIC. Lesson 23 compares them, and shows why priors, not stepwise rules, are the natural way to handle many candidate predictors.



Further reading: Heinze et al. (2018) review variable selection and its pitfalls; Greenland (1989) on modeling strategy in epidemiology; Harrell (2015) on the problems of stepwise selection.

Residual patterns over time, residual autocorrelation and overdispersion show what a model is missing.

title: Lesson 8 · Generalized linear models: logistic and Poisson regression
section: 8.1 Three ingredients: distribution, link, linear predictor
text:
8.1 Three ingredients: distribution, link, linear predictor
A GLM has a linear predictor, η = α + βx, exactly as in linear regression. A link function connects η to the mean, so the mean stays in its allowed range: the log link keeps counts positive, the logit link keeps probabilities between 0 and 1. And a distribution describes how observations scatter around the mean. Change α and β and see the same linear predictor through three links.


  Intercept α
  Slope β
  
  identity: mean = ηlog: mean = eηlogit: mean = 1 / (1 + e−η)






AStandard notation

\[Y_i \sim \text{distribution}(\mu_i), \qquad g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \alpha + \beta x_i\]

Linear regression: normal, \(g(\mu) = \mu\). Logistic: Bernoulli, \(g(\pi) = \log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\). Poisson: \(g(\mu) = \log\mu\).




BModel list and R

glm(y ~ x, family = gaussian)              # identity
glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
glm(y ~ x, family = poisson(link = "log"))



CHow it’s reported

Coefficients are reported on the scale that makes sense for the link: as differences for the identity link, odds ratios \(e^{\beta}\) for the logit link, and rate ratios \(e^{\beta}\) for the log link.



Further reading: McCullagh and Nelder (1989) is the original book-length treatment of GLMs; Agresti (2013) and Fox (2016) give accessible introductions.
crumbs: Lesson 8 · Generalized linear models: logistic and Poisson regression

title: Lesson 8 · Generalized linear models: logistic and Poisson regression
text:
8.2 Logistic regression and odds ratios
Logistic regression models the log-odds of asthma as a linear function of NO₂ and other variables. Its slope, exponentiated, is an odds ratio. Because a 1 µg/m³ change is trivial, report the OR per a meaningful unit, such as 10 µg/m³ or an interquartile range. Compare the crude and adjusted estimates, and the estimate using modeled NO₂ with the one using the true exposure, known here only because the data are simulated.


  Report per10 µg/m³1 µg/m³interquartile range
  Exposuremodeled NO₂ (what a real study has)true NO₂ (simulation only)
   adjust for SES, parental smoking, green space and sex
  
  observed risk in tenths of NO₂fitted logistic curve






AStandard notation

\[Y_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)\] \[\mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = \alpha + \beta\,\frac{\mathrm{NO}_{2,i}}{10} + \gamma^\top z_i, \qquad OR_{10} = e^{\beta}\]



BModel list and R

asthma[i] ~ bernoulli(p[i])
logit(p[i]) = a + b * no2[i] / 10 + g * z[i]

fit <- glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses +
             parent_smoke + green + sex,
           family = binomial, data = cohort)
broom::tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE,
            conf.int = TRUE)



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Reporting an OR per 1 µg/m³ (for example 1.014) with too few decimals, so it reads as “no effect”, or presenting an adjusted OR for a common outcome as if it were a risk ratio. Choose a meaningful unit, and estimate risk ratios directly when the outcome is common.








NoteR code (optional): logistic regression, and risk ratios by modified Poisson






fit_crude <- glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10), family = binomial, data = cohort)
fit_adj   <- glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + parent_smoke + green + sex,
                 family = binomial, data = cohort)
bind_rows(crude = broom::tidy(fit_crude, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)[2, ],
          adjusted = broom::tidy(fit_adj, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)[2, ],
          .id = "model")

#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   model    term          estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>    <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 crude    I(no2_modele…     1.23    0.0374     5.65  1.64e-8    1.15       1.33
#> 2 adjusted I(no2_modele…     1.05    0.0559     0.839 4.01e-1    0.939      1.17

# risk ratio per 10 ug/m3: Poisson model with robust (sandwich) standard errors
fit_rr <- glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + parent_smoke + green + sex,
              family = poisson, data = cohort)
rr_se <- sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(fit_rr, type = "HC0")))[2]
exp(coef(fit_rr)[2] + c(estimate = 0, low = -1.96, high = 1.96) * rr_se)

#>  estimate       low      high 
#> 1.0405772 0.9485384 1.1415466






Further reading: Hosmer et al. (2013) is the standard text on logistic regression; Zou (2004) introduced modified Poisson regression for risk ratios; Altman et al. (1998) on why odds ratios mislead for common outcomes.

section: 8.3 Poisson regression for rates: the offset
text:
8.3 Poisson regression for rates: the offset
District rates of emergency visits depend on age structure and deprivation. A Poisson regression of visit counts must account for how many person-years each count comes from. That is the role of the offset: log(person-years) enters the model with a coefficient fixed at 1, so the model describes rates, not raw counts. Each row below is one district and age group over five years. Remove the offset and see what goes wrong.


   include log(person-years) as an offset
   include district deprivation
  






AStandard notation

\[D_{jk} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{jk})\] \[\log \mu_{jk} = \log PT_{jk} + \alpha + \gamma_k + \beta\,\mathrm{dep}_j\]

\(j\) = district, \(k\) = age group. \(e^{\gamma_k}\) and \(e^{\beta}\) are rate ratios.




BModel list and R

D[j,k] ~ poisson(mu[j,k])
log(mu[j,k]) = log(PT[j,k]) + a + g[k] + b * dep[j]

agg <- visits |>
  group_by(district_id, age_group) |>
  summarise(D = sum(visits),
            PT = sum(population) / 365.25) |>
  left_join(districts, by = "district_id")
glm(D ~ age_group + deprivation + offset(log(PT)),
    family = poisson, data = agg)



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): rate ratios from a Poisson model with an offset






agg <- visits |>
  group_by(district_id, age_group) |>
  summarise(D = sum(visits), PT = sum(population) / 365.25, .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(districts, by = "district_id") |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("0-14", "15-64", "65+"), ordered = FALSE))

fit_rate <- glm(D ~ age_group + deprivation + offset(log(PT)), family = poisson, data = agg)
broom::tidy(fit_rate, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

#>   term           estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)       0.199   0.00404    -399.        0    0.198     0.201
#> 2 age_group15-64    0.823   0.00328     -59.4       0    0.817     0.828
#> 3 age_group65+      1.84    0.00355     172.        0    1.83      1.86 
#> 4 deprivation       1.41    0.00593      58.0       0    1.39      1.43






Further reading: Frome and Checkoway (1985) on Poisson regression for incidence rates; Clayton and Hills (1993) on rates, person-time and log-linear models; Cameron and Trivedi (2013) on count models.

title: Lesson 8 · Generalized linear models: logistic and Poisson regression
text:
8.4 Overdispersion and quasi-Poisson standard errors
A Poisson model assumes the variance equals the mean. Daily emergency counts vary more (Lesson 3). The coefficients are still estimated correctly, but their standard errors are too small. The quasi-Poisson model estimates a dispersion parameter φ and multiplies every standard error by √φ. Here the question is the effect of PM2.5 on daily visits, adjusted for season and day of the week.


  Serieswhole city, all agesOld Town, 65+Lakeside, 0–14
   adjust for season and day of week
  






AStandard notation

\[E[Y_t] = \mu_t, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \phi\,\mu_t\] \[\hat\phi = \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_t \frac{(y_t - \hat\mu_t)^2}{\hat\mu_t}, \qquad SE_{\text{quasi}} = \sqrt{\hat\phi}\,SE_{\text{Poisson}}\]



BModel list and R

glm(visits ~ I(pm25 / 10) + sin(2*pi*doy/365.25) +
      cos(2*pi*doy/365.25) + dow,
    family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



In a Bayesian model, overdispersion is handled by choosing a negative binomial likelihood, whose extra parameter is estimated with everything else, or by adding a random effect for each day. Posterior predictive checks (Lesson 22) reveal overdispersion the model misses.



Further reading: Ver Hoef and Boveng (2007) compare quasi-Poisson with negative binomial models; McCullagh and Nelder (1989) introduced quasi-likelihood for GLMs; Agresti (2013) discusses overdispersion in count and binary data.

title: Lesson 8 · Generalized linear models: logistic and Poisson regression
text:
Key takeaways

A GLM = a distribution + a link function + a linear predictor. Linear, logistic and Poisson regression are all GLMs.
In logistic regression, \(e^{\beta}\) is an odds ratio. Report it per a meaningful unit of exposure.
For common outcomes, estimate risk ratios directly (for example, Poisson regression with robust standard errors).
In Poisson regression for rates, log(person-time) is an offset. Without it, a model describes counts, not rates.
Overdispersion leaves estimates unbiased but makes Poisson standard errors too small; quasi-Poisson or negative binomial models fix this.

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text:
6.1 Confidence intervals and coverage
Each simulated study draws a sample of children and computes a 95% confidence interval for the risk of asthma. The true risk in the whole cohort is known. A 95% interval comes from a procedure that, across many studies, captures the truth 95% of the time. Any single interval either contains it or doesn’t. Run 100 studies and count the misses.


  Children per study
  Confidence level80%90%95%99%
  Run 100 new studies
  
  interval contains the truthinterval missestrue risk






AStandard notation

\[\hat\pi \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)}{n}}\] \[P_\pi\big(L \le \pi \le U\big) = 1 - \alpha \ \text{ for every } \pi\]

\(z_{0.975} = 1.96\) for a 95% interval. The probability statement is about the procedure, over repeated samples.




BModel list and R

smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 200)
p  <- mean(smp$asthma)
se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 200)
p + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se

binom.test(sum(smp$asthma), 200)$conf.int



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



“There is a 95% probability that the true risk lies between 9% and 18%.” For a confidence interval, the 95% describes the method, not this interval. The statement in quotes is what a Bayesian credible interval says (Lesson 19).



Further reading: Gardner and Altman (1986) argued for reporting confidence intervals rather than p-values; Greenland et al. (2016) list common misinterpretations of intervals; Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) derive intervals for risks and rates.
crumbs: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text:
6.2 Hypothesis tests and p-values
A test asks: if there were truly no effect, how surprising would data like ours be? The p-value is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. To see its behavior, run many studies comparing asthma risk between two groups. First use a fake “exposure” assigned by coin toss, so the null is true; then the real exposure, high modeled NO₂.


  Coin-toss exposure (null true)High NO₂, ≥ 30 µg/m³
  Children per study
  Run 1,000 studies
  






AStandard notation

\[H_0: \pi_1 = \pi_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_1: \pi_1 \ne \pi_0\] \[z = \frac{\hat\pi_1 - \hat\pi_0}{\sqrt{\bar\pi(1-\bar\pi)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_0}\right)}}, \qquad p = 2\,P(Z \ge |z|)\]



BModel list and R

smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 500) |>
  mutate(high = no2_modeled >= 30)
prop.test(table(smp$high, smp$asthma)[, 2:1],
          correct = FALSE)



CHow it’s reported



Report the effect estimate with its confidence interval and the exact p-value, not only “p < 0.05”.









NoteR code (optional): p-values under the null and under a real effect






set.seed(6)
one_study <- function(n, real = TRUE) {
  smp <- slice_sample(cohort, n = n)
  expo <- if (real) smp$no2_modeled >= 30 else runif(n) < 0.5
  prop.test(c(sum(smp$asthma[expo]), sum(smp$asthma[!expo])),
            c(sum(expo), sum(!expo)), correct = FALSE)$p.value
}
p_null <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_study(500, real = FALSE))
p_real <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_study(500, real = TRUE))
c(null_below_0.05 = mean(p_null < 0.05), real_below_0.05 = mean(p_real < 0.05))

#> null_below_0.05 real_below_0.05 
#>           0.048           0.258






Further reading: Wasserstein and Lazar (2016) is the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values; Greenland et al. (2016) explain 25 common misinterpretations; Matthews and Altman (1996) on comparing effect sizes rather than p-values.
crumbs: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text:
6.3 Errors, power and exaggerated estimates
Rejecting a true null is a type I error, with probability α. Missing a real effect is a type II error. Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size, and it depends on the effect, the baseline risk, the sample size and α. Small studies have low power, and there is a second, less obvious problem: when a low-powered study does reach significance, its estimate tends to be far too large.


  True risk ratio
  Children per group
  Significance level α0.010.050.10
  
  Simulate 2,000 studies at this size









WarningCommon pitfall



Treating a significant result from a small study as a reliable estimate of the effect. Among the studies that pass p < 0.05, the estimates are biased upward, often severely. This “winner’s curse” is one reason early findings shrink when replicated.



Further reading: Button et al. (2013) show how low power undermines reliability, including the exaggeration of significant effects; Greenland et al. (2016) on misinterpretations of power; Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) give sample size and power calculations for epidemiological comparisons.
crumbs: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text:
6.4 Multiple testing
Test twenty exposures that have no effect at all, each at α = 0.05, and you expect one “significant” result by chance alone. The chance of at least one false positive is 64%. A Bonferroni correction divides α by the number of tests, at a cost in power. Whether to correct depends on the question: confirming a single pre-specified hypothesis, or exploring many.


  Number of null exposures tested
   Apply a Bonferroni correction
  Run one study with these testsRepeat 1,000 times
  






AStandard notation

\[P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1-\alpha)^m\] \[\text{Bonferroni: reject } H_{0j} \text{ if } p_j < \alpha / m\]



BModel list and R

p_values <- c(0.003, 0.02, 0.04, 0.30)
p.adjust(p_values, method = "bonferroni")
p.adjust(p_values, method = "holm")



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Bender and Lange (2001) explain when and how to adjust for multiple testing; Rothman (1990) argues that adjustment is often unnecessary when results are interpreted with care; Greenland et al. (2016) place both views in context.
crumbs: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text:
6.5 Absence of evidence and equivalence
A non-significant result means the data are compatible with no effect. They may also be compatible with a large effect. “Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.” To support the claim that an effect is negligible, set a margin in advance, here a risk ratio between 0.9 and 1.1, and check whether the confidence interval lies entirely inside it. Move the estimate and its precision and watch the four possible conclusions.


  Estimated risk ratio
  Standard error of log RR
  Equivalence margin (±)
  









TipBayesian preview



A frequentist test can reject “no effect” but can never support it; that needs the separate equivalence test above. A Bayesian analysis can state the probability that the effect lies inside the margin (a “region of practical equivalence”), and a Bayes factor can weigh “no effect” against “some effect” directly. Lesson 23 compares the approaches.



Further reading: Altman and Bland (1995) on why a non-significant result is not evidence of no effect; Lakens (2017) is a practical primer on equivalence tests (TOST); Greenland et al. (2016) on interpreting non-significant results.

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text: Check your understanding

title: Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
text:
Key takeaways

A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the truth in 95% of studies. Its width shows precision.
A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor a measure of effect size.
Under a true null, p-values are uniformly distributed: 5% fall below 0.05 by chance.
Power depends on effect size, baseline risk, sample size and α. Significant results from low-powered studies exaggerate effects.
Testing many hypotheses inflates false positives; correct when confirming, interpret carefully when exploring.
Non-significant does not mean no effect. To support “no meaningful effect”, use an equivalence margin.

title: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
4.1 Population, sample and estimate
Treat the 1,827 days of the city’s emergency department record as the population. Its mean, the true average number of visits per day, is the parameter we want, and here we happen to know it. A study can only afford to look at some days: a sample. The sample mean is an estimator; its value in one sample is an estimate. Draw samples and watch the estimates scatter around the truth.


  Days per sample, n
  Draw 1 sampleDraw 100 samplesDraw 1,000 samplesStart over
  
  sample means so fartrue population meanthe latest sample




Further reading: Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) on populations, samples and sampling variation; Casella and Berger (2002) on estimators and their properties; Lash et al. (2021) on random and systematic error in epidemiology.
crumbs: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem

title: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
4.2 The standard error
The spread of the sampling distribution is the standard error (SE). It says how far a typical estimate lies from the truth. For a mean, it equals the population SD divided by √n: to halve the SE you need four times as many observations. The curve shows the SE for every sample size; the dot is where your current n sits, and the cross is the spread actually observed among your simulated samples.







AStandard notation

\[SE(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \widehat{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

\(\sigma\) = population SD, \(s\) = sample SD, \(n\) = sample size.




BModel list and R

smp <- city_daily |> slice_sample(n = 20)
smp |>
  summarise(mean = mean(visits),
            sd   = sd(visits),
            se   = sd / sqrt(n()))



CHow it’s reported



Report the SD to describe the data and the SE (or better, a confidence interval) to describe the estimate.









WarningCommon pitfall



Reporting “mean ± SE” to describe variability in the data. The SE shrinks as the sample grows, so it makes data look less variable than they are. Use the SD to describe the data and the SE for the precision of the mean.








NoteR code (optional): simulating the sampling distribution






city_daily <- visits |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(visits = sum(visits), pm25 = first(pm25), .groups = "drop")

set.seed(1)
sample_means <- map_dbl(1:2000, \(i) mean(slice_sample(city_daily, n = 20)$visits))

tibble(true_mean = mean(city_daily$visits),
       mean_of_estimates = mean(sample_means),
       empirical_se = sd(sample_means),
       theoretical_se = sd(city_daily$visits) / sqrt(20))

#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   true_mean mean_of_estimates empirical_se theoretical_se
#>       <dbl>             <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1      435.              435.         17.4           17.7






Further reading: Altman and Bland (2005) explain the difference between standard deviations and standard errors; Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) derive the standard error of a mean and of a proportion.

title: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
4.3 The central limit theorem
Daily PM2.5 is right-skewed. Yet if you average enough days, the averages follow a nearly normal distribution: this is the central limit theorem. It is why so many intervals use 1.96. How many days are “enough” depends on how skewed the data are. Change the number of days averaged.


  Variabledaily PM2.5 (right-skewed)daily visits, Lakeside 0–14 (small counts)daily temperature (two peaks)
  n = 1251030100
  
  2,000 averages of n daysnormal curve with the same mean and SD




Further reading: Casella and Berger (2002) state and prove the central limit theorem; Blitzstein and Hwang (2019) give an accessible treatment; Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) discuss when the normal approximation is adequate.
crumbs: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem

title: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
section: 4.4 The bootstrap: a standard error from one sample
text:
4.4 The bootstrap: a standard error from one sample
In a real study there is only one sample. The bootstrap imitates repeated sampling by resampling from the sample itself, with replacement, many times, and recomputing the estimate each time. The spread of these bootstrap estimates approximates the standard error. Here, one sample of 30 children estimates mean residential NO₂.


  Children in the sample
  Draw a new study sampleRun 2,000 bootstrap resamples
  
  bootstrap meansthe sample's own meantrue mean in all 5,000 children






AStandard notation

\[y^{*(b)} \sim \text{resample}(y_1, \dots, y_n), \quad b = 1, \dots, B\] \[\widehat{SE}_{\text{boot}} = \mathrm{SD}\big(\hat\theta^{*(1)}, \dots, \hat\theta^{*(B)}\big)\]



BModel list and R

smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 30)
boot <- map_dbl(1:2000, \(b)
  mean(sample(smp$no2_modeled, replace = TRUE)))
sd(boot)                         # bootstrap SE
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))  # percentile CI



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): a bootstrap standard error






set.seed(2)
smp  <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 30)
boot <- map_dbl(1:2000, \(b) mean(sample(smp$no2_modeled, replace = TRUE)))

tibble(estimate     = mean(smp$no2_modeled),
       se_formula   = sd(smp$no2_modeled) / sqrt(30),
       se_bootstrap = sd(boot),
       ci_low       = quantile(boot, 0.025),
       ci_high      = quantile(boot, 0.975))

#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   estimate se_formula se_bootstrap ci_low ci_high
#>      <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1     28.2       2.17         2.13   24.0    32.1











TipBayesian preview



The sampling distribution is a frequentist idea: it describes what would happen across studies you never ran. A Bayesian instead describes uncertainty about the parameter given the one sample you have, with a posterior distribution. With little prior information and enough data, the two give similar intervals; Lesson 19 shows when and why they differ.



Further reading: Efron (1979) introduced the bootstrap; Efron and Tibshirani (1993) is the standard book; Carpenter and Bithell (2000) is a practical guide to bootstrap confidence intervals for medical statisticians.

title: Lesson 4 · Sampling, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
Key takeaways

A parameter is fixed; an estimate varies from sample to sample. The sampling distribution describes that variation.
The standard error is the SD of the sampling distribution. For a mean, SE = σ/√n.
The SD describes the data; the SE describes the precision of an estimate. They answer different questions.
Averages of many values are approximately normal (central limit theorem), sooner for symmetric data than for skewed data.
The bootstrap estimates a standard error from a single sample by resampling it.

title: Lesson 2 · Probability and conditional probability
text:
2.1 Probability and its rules
A probability is a number between 0 and 1. In a cohort, the probability of an event is estimated by the proportion of children who experience it. Two events can be combined: both happen (the intersection, written A ∩ B), or at least one happens (the union, A ∪ B). Choose two events in the asthma cohort. The mosaic plot divides the children into the four combinations, with each area proportional to the number of children.


  Event B
    a parent smokes at home
    modeled NO₂ at least 30 µg/m³
    the child is a boy
    the wheeze questionnaire is positive
  Event A is always "the child develops asthma by age 8".
  
  asthma (A)no asthma






AStandard notation

\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\] \[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\] \[\text{independent} \iff P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)\]



BModel list and R

cohort |>
  summarise(
    p_A       = mean(asthma),
    p_B       = mean(parent_smoke),
    p_AandB   = mean(asthma & parent_smoke),
    p_AorB    = mean(asthma | parent_smoke),
    p_A_givB  = mean(asthma[parent_smoke]),
    p_A_givnB = mean(asthma[!parent_smoke]))



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Blitzstein and Hwang (2019) develop probability from first principles; Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) introduce it for medical statistics; Clayton and Hills (1993) connect probability to epidemiological models.

title: Lesson 2 · Probability and conditional probability
text:
2.2 Conditional probability and independence
Conditioning restricts attention to the children for whom one event is true. In the mosaic plot, P(A | B) is the height of the orange part in the left column, and P(A | not B) in the right column. If the two heights are equal, knowing B tells you nothing about A: the events are independent. If they differ, the events are associated. Association between an exposure and an outcome is exactly what epidemiology measures; the risk ratio from Lesson 1 is P(A | B) / P(A | not B).
The order of conditioning matters. P(asthma | positive questionnaire) and P(positive questionnaire | asthma) are different numbers, and the next section shows how far apart they can be. Switch event B to the questionnaire and compare them.







NoteR code (optional): joint and conditional probabilities






cohort |>
  count(parent_smoke, asthma) |>
  mutate(p_joint = n / sum(n)) |>
  group_by(parent_smoke) |>
  mutate(p_asthma_given_smoke = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   parent_smoke asthma     n p_joint p_asthma_given_smoke
#>   <lgl>         <dbl> <int>   <dbl>                <dbl>
#> 1 FALSE             0  3385  0.677                 0.879
#> 2 FALSE             1   465  0.093                 0.121
#> 3 TRUE              0   929  0.186                 0.808
#> 4 TRUE              1   221  0.0442                0.192

# independence would make these two equal
with(cohort, c(p_A = mean(asthma),
               p_A_given_B = mean(asthma[parent_smoke])))

#>         p_A p_A_given_B 
#>   0.1372000   0.1921739






Further reading: Blitzstein and Hwang (2019) on conditioning and independence; Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) show that natural frequencies make conditional reasoning much easier; Lash et al. (2021) on measures of association as contrasts of conditional risks.

title: Lesson 2 · Probability and conditional probability
text:
2.3 Bayes’ theorem and diagnostic tests
The wheeze questionnaire is used to screen for asthma. Its sensitivity is the probability of a positive result in a child with asthma; its specificity the probability of a negative result in a child without. Parents and doctors want the reverse: given a positive result, how likely is asthma? That is the positive predictive value (PPV), and Bayes’ theorem gives it. The icon array shows 1,000 children; change the prevalence, sensitivity and specificity.


  Prevalence
  Sensitivity
  Specificity
  Use the values observed in the cohortA rare condition (1%)
  
  true positivefalse negativefalse positivetrue negative


  
  
  





AStandard notation

\[Se = P(T^+ \mid D^+) \qquad Sp = P(T^- \mid D^-)\] \[PPV = P(D^+ \mid T^+) = \frac{Se \cdot p}{Se \cdot p + (1 - Sp)(1 - p)}\]

\(p\) = prevalence, \(D^+\) = has asthma, \(T^+\) = positive test.




BModel list and R

cohort |>
  summarise(
    sens = mean(wheeze_q[asthma == 1]),
    spec = mean(!wheeze_q[asthma == 0]),
    ppv  = mean(asthma[wheeze_q]),
    npv  = mean(1 - asthma[!wheeze_q]))



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Reading sensitivity as the probability that a positive child has the condition. With a prevalence of 1%, a test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity gives a PPV of only about 8%: more than nine in ten positives are false. Try the “rare condition” button.








NoteR code (optional): diagnostic accuracy in the cohort






cohort |>
  count(wheeze_q, asthma) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = asthma, values_from = n, names_prefix = "asthma_")

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   wheeze_q asthma_0 asthma_1
#>   <lgl>       <int>    <int>
#> 1 FALSE        3900      122
#> 2 TRUE          414      564

cohort |>
  summarise(sens = mean(wheeze_q[asthma == 1]),
            spec = mean(!wheeze_q[asthma == 0]),
            ppv  = mean(asthma[wheeze_q]),
            npv  = mean(1 - asthma[!wheeze_q]))

#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>    sens  spec   ppv   npv
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.822 0.904 0.577 0.970






Further reading: Altman and Bland (1994a) and Altman and Bland (1994b) are short classics on sensitivity, specificity and predictive values; Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) and Hoffrage et al. (2000) show how natural frequencies, like the tree above, prevent errors.

title: Lesson 2 · Probability and conditional probability
text:
2.4 Likelihood ratios: updating a probability
Bayes’ theorem has an especially simple form on the odds scale. A likelihood ratio says how many times more likely a test result is in children with asthma than without. Multiply the pre-test odds by it, and you get the post-test odds. This is updating: start from what you believed before the test, and let the evidence move you. The same logic, applied to parameters instead of diagnoses, is the core of Bayesian statistics (Part V).


  Pre-test probability
  Sensitivity
  Specificity
  
  after a positive resultafter a negative resultno test






AStandard notation

\[LR^+ = \frac{Se}{1 - Sp} \qquad LR^- = \frac{1 - Se}{Sp}\] \[\text{post-test odds} = \text{pre-test odds} \times LR\]



BModel list and R

lr_pos    <- sens / (1 - spec)
pre_odds  <- p_pre / (1 - p_pre)
post_odds <- pre_odds * lr_pos
p_post    <- post_odds / (1 + post_odds)



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



Replace “has asthma” with “the true effect of NO₂ is β” and “test result” with “the data”. Bayes’ theorem then turns a prior belief about β and the likelihood of the data into a posterior belief: \(p(\beta \mid \text{data}) \propto p(\text{data} \mid \beta)\, p(\beta)\). The pre-test probability becomes the prior, the likelihood ratio becomes the likelihood, and the post-test probability becomes the posterior. Lesson 19 builds this up step by step.



Further reading: Deeks and Altman (2004) explain likelihood ratios for test results; Bland and Altman (1998) contrast Bayesian and frequentist reasoning in a page; Held and Sabanés Bové (2020) develop likelihood and Bayesian inference together.
