title: Lesson 2 · Probability and conditional probability
text:
Key takeaways

Probabilities of combined events follow simple rules: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
P(A | B) restricts attention to cases where B is true. P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different.
Events are independent when conditioning on one doesn’t change the probability of the other. An exposure–outcome association is a departure from independence.
Bayes’ theorem reverses a conditional probability. Predictive values depend strongly on prevalence.
On the odds scale, updating is a multiplication by the likelihood ratio, the simplest form of Bayesian reasoning.

text:
Example B · Traffic-related air pollution and childhood asthma
A birth cohort of 5,000 children living in the same districts, followed to age 8. Each child has a modeled residential NO₂ level from a land-use regression model, as in most real studies. A validation subsample of children also wore personal NO₂ monitors. We know their socio-economic position, parental smoking, residential green space, school, a parent-reported wheeze questionnaire, and whether they were diagnosed with asthma by age 8.

Notice how NO₂ and socio-economic position travel together across districts. Untangling them is the subject of Lessons 9 and 12.

section: Three ways of writing the same thing
text:
Three ways of writing the same thing
Statistical models appear in three forms, and you’ll need all three. Papers and textbooks use standard notation. Software uses a model list, one line per assumption, written in R. And results are communicated in epidemiological reporting style. Throughout the course, the three appear side by side so you can translate between them. Here is the model that actually generated the asthma data in Example B. Don’t worry about understanding it yet; by Lesson 18 you will.



AStandard notation

\[Y_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)\] \[\mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = \alpha + \beta\,\frac{\mathrm{NO}_{2,i} - 25}{10} + \gamma_1 \mathrm{SES}_i + \gamma_2\, \mathrm{smoke}_i + \gamma_3\, \mathrm{green}_i + \gamma_4\, \mathrm{boy}_i + u_{s[i]}\] \[u_s \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_u^2)\]

\(Y_i\) = asthma by age 8 for child \(i\), \(\pi_i\) its probability, \(s[i]\) the child’s school.




BModel list and R

asthma    ~ bernoulli(p)
logit(p)  = alpha + beta * (no2 - 25) / 10 +
            g1 * ses + g2 * smoke +
            g3 * green + g4 * boy + u[school]
u[school] ~ normal(0, sigma_u)

# in R (Lesson 18):
glmer(asthma ~ I((no2 - 25) / 10) + ses +
        parent_smoke + green + sex + (1 | school),
      family = binomial, data = cohort)



CHow it’s reported

Each 10 µg/m³ increase in residential NO₂ was associated with 15% higher odds of asthma by age 8 (OR 1.15 per 10 µg/m³), adjusted for socio-economic position, parental smoking, green space and sex, and accounting for clustering within schools.

Here these numbers are the truth, known because the data are simulated. In a real study they would be estimates with confidence or credible intervals.



The symbols are used consistently in every lesson: \(\alpha\) for intercepts and baselines, \(\beta\) for exposure effects, \(\gamma\) for adjustment terms, \(u\) for group effects, \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) for standard deviations, and the indices \(i\) (child), \(t\) (day), \(j\) (district or school) and \(\ell\) (lag). The glossary keeps the full list.

text:
Symbols and notation
Every model is shown three ways side by side: A, standard notation, as in papers and textbooks; B, a model list with R, one line per assumption, as in software; and C, epidemiological reporting, as in a results section.







Symbol
Meaning




\(Y_i\), \(y_t\)
Outcome for child \(i\), or count on day \(t\)


\(\alpha\)
Intercept or baseline (log or logit scale)


\(\beta\), \(\beta_\ell\)
Exposure effects; the effect at lag \(\ell\)


\(\gamma\)
Adjustment (confounder) terms


\(u_j\)
Group effect for district or school \(j\)


\(\sigma\), \(\tau\)
Residual and between-group standard deviations


\(\pi_i\), \(\mu_t\)
Probability of the outcome for child \(i\); expected count on day \(t\)


\(i, t, j, k, \ell\)
Indices: child, day, district or school, age group, lag

Cases, people at risk, person-time


\(R\), \(O\), \(I\)
Risk, odds, incidence rate

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
A

Additive and multiplicative interaction (RERI)
Causal inference
Interaction can be present on the risk-difference (additive) scale and absent on the ratio (multiplicative) scale, or the reverse.
Additive interaction is usually more relevant for public health, because it tells you where an intervention prevents the most cases. Logistic and Poisson models test multiplicative interaction.

Formal definition. \(RERI = RR_{11} - RR_{10} - RR_{01} + 1\); additive interaction when \(RERI \ne 0\), multiplicative when \(RR_{11} \ne RR_{10} RR_{01}\).

Related: Effect modification, Interaction, Risk difference (RD) · Lessons: 9


Adjusted odds ratio (aOR)
Epidemiological measures
An odds ratio from a model that includes other variables, usually confounders.
The aOR compares the odds of the outcome between people who differ in the exposure but have the same values of the adjustment variables. It is a conditional effect: it applies within levels of the covariates, not to the population as a whole.

Formal definition. In \(\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \gamma^\top z_i\), \(aOR = e^{\beta}\), the OR for a one-unit increase in \(x\) holding \(z\) fixed.


In epidemiology. Always state which variables were adjusted for. An aOR is only as good as the adjustment set (directed acyclic graph), and because of non-collapsibility it can differ from the crude OR even without confounding.


In R:
glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + parent_smoke + green + sex, family = binomial, data = cohort)


How it’s reported. “aOR 1.12 per 10 µg/m³ (95% CI 1.01 to 1.24), adjusted for socio-economic position, parental smoking, green space and sex”

Related: Odds ratio (OR), Crude and adjusted estimates, Confounding, Non-collapsibility · Lessons: 8, 9, 12


Adjustment set
Causal inference
A set of variables that, when adjusted for, blocks all backdoor paths and opens no new ones.
Related: Directed acyclic graph (DAG), Backdoor path, Confounder · Lessons: 9


Age-specific rate
Standardization
A rate calculated separately within one age group.
Age-specific rates remove age structure from the comparison within each group. Standardization combines them into one number using common weights.

Formal definition. \(r_{jk} = D_{jk} / PT_{jk}\) for district \(j\) and age group \(k\).

Related: Crude rate, Direct standardization (age-standardized rate, ASR) · Lessons: 1


Akaike information criterion (AIC)
Model building
A score for comparing models that rewards fit and penalizes complexity. Lower is better.
Only differences matter: ΔAIC below about 2 means the models are similarly supported, above 10 means the worse one has essentially no support. Models must be fitted to the same data.

Formal definition. \(AIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + 2k\), with \(k\) parameters. It estimates relative out-of-sample predictive performance.


In R:
AIC(fit0, fit1, fit2)

Related: Quasi-AIC (QAIC), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), Likelihood ratio test (LRT), Widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) · Lessons: 10


Alternative hypothesis (H1)
Testing and intervals
The hypothesis that is supported when the null is rejected.
It can be two-sided (\(\beta \neq 0\)) or one-sided (\(\beta > 0\)). The choice must be made before seeing the data.
Related: Null hypothesis (H0), One-sided and two-sided tests · Lessons: 6


Areal data
Spatial
Data aggregated over areas, such as visits per district.
Related: Point-referenced data, Disease mapping, Spatial autocorrelation · Lessons: 17


Attributable fraction among the exposed (AFe)
Disease burden
The fraction of cases among exposed people that is due to the exposure.
If the exposure doubles the risk, half the exposed cases would not have occurred without it.

Formal definition. \(AF_e = (RR - 1) / RR\).

Related: Population attributable fraction (PAF), Risk ratio (RR) · Lessons: 14


Attributable number (AN)
Disease burden
The number of cases attributable to an exposure: the PAF times the total number of cases.
For time-varying exposures like temperature, attributable numbers are computed day by day and summed, with uncertainty obtained by simulation.

Formal definition. \(AN = PAF \times D\). For daily data, \(AN = \sum_t D_t \left(1 - 1/RR(x_t)\right)\), the backward perspective used in DLNM studies.

Related: Population attributable fraction (PAF), Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM) · Lessons: 14, 16


Autocorrelation
Time series
Correlation of a series with itself at earlier times: today resembles yesterday.
Residual autocorrelation means the model hasn’t captured all time patterns. It makes standard errors too small. The ACF plot shows the correlation at each lag.

Formal definition. \(\rho(k) = \mathrm{Corr}(Y_t, Y_{t-k})\), estimated by \(\hat{\rho}(k) = \frac{\sum_t (y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t-k} - \bar{y})}{\sum_t (y_t - \bar{y})^2}\).


In R:
acf(residuals(fit, type = "pearson"))

Related: Time-series study, Independence, Spatial autocorrelation · Lessons: 15


Average causal effect (ATE)
Causal inference
The difference (or ratio) in average outcome if everyone were exposed versus if no one were.

Formal definition. \(ATE = E[Y^1] - E[Y^0]\); causal risk ratio \(E[Y^1]/E[Y^0]\). The effect in the exposed (ATT) averages over the exposed only.

Related: Potential outcomes, G-computation (standardization), Inverse probability weighting (IPW) · Lessons: 12

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
B

Backdoor path
Causal inference
A non-causal path from exposure to outcome that starts with an arrow into the exposure.
Open backdoor paths create confounding. They are blocked by adjusting for a non-collider on the path.
Related: Directed acyclic graph (DAG), Confounding, Adjustment set · Lessons: 9


Bayes factor
Bayesian model comparison
The ratio of how well two models or hypotheses predicted the observed data.
BF₁₀ = 10 means the data are 10 times more probable under H1 than under H0. Bayes factors can support the null, compare non-nested models and weigh many hypotheses at once, but they depend strongly on the priors within each hypothesis.

Formal definition. \(BF_{10} = \frac{p(y \mid H_1)}{p(y \mid H_0)}\), and posterior odds = \(BF_{10}\) × prior odds.


How it’s reported. Labels (Lee & Wagenmakers): 1–3 anecdotal, 3–10 moderate, 10–30 strong, 30–100 very strong, >100 extreme.

Related: Marginal likelihood (evidence), Savage–Dickey density ratio, Lindley’s paradox, Posterior model probability · Lessons: 23


Bayes’ theorem
Probability
The rule for reversing a conditional probability: from P(B | A) to P(A | B).
In diagnostic testing it turns sensitivity and prevalence into the positive predictive value. In Bayesian statistics, applied to parameters, it gives the posterior distribution from the prior distribution and the likelihood.

Formal definition. \[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\] For parameters \(\theta\) and data \(y\): \(p(\theta \mid y) \propto p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\).

Related: Conditional probability, Positive predictive value (PPV), Posterior distribution, Prior distribution, Likelihood · Lessons: 2, 19


Bayesian inference
Bayesian basics
Inference that describes unknown parameters with probability distributions, updated from prior to posterior by the data.

Formal definition. \(p(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(y)} \propto p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)\).

Related: Prior distribution, Posterior distribution, Likelihood, Bayes’ theorem · Lessons: 19


Bayesian information criterion (BIC)
Model building
A model comparison score like AIC, with a stronger penalty for complexity. Lower is better.

Formal definition. \(BIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + k\log n\). Differences in BIC approximate \(-2\log\) of a Bayes factor under particular priors.

Related: Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayes factor · Lessons: 10


Berkson error
Measurement error
Error in which the true value varies around the assigned value, as when everyone in an area is given the area average.
Assigning each child their district’s mean NO₂ creates Berkson error. In linear models it causes little bias but wider confidence intervals; in nonlinear models it can bias.

Formal definition. \(X = W + U\), \(U \perp W\), \(E[U] = 0\).

Related: Classical measurement error, Measurement error · Lessons: 13


Bernoulli distribution
Distributions
The distribution of a single yes/no outcome with probability π of “yes”.

Formal definition. \(P(Y = 1) = \pi\), \(P(Y = 0) = 1 - \pi\); \(E[Y] = \pi\), \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \pi(1 - \pi)\).

Related: Binomial distribution, Binary variable, Logistic regression · Lessons: 3, 8


Beta distribution
Distributions
A distribution for quantities between 0 and 1, such as a risk or a proportion.

Formal definition. \(f(\pi) = \frac{\pi^{a-1}(1-\pi)^{b-1}}{B(a, b)}\), \(0 < \pi < 1\), with mean \(a/(a+b)\). It is the conjugate prior for a binomial probability.

Related: Conjugate prior, Binomial distribution · Lessons: 19


Bias
Sampling and estimation
A systematic difference between what an estimate targets and the truth.
Statistical bias is a property of an estimator: on average across repeated samples, it misses the truth. In epidemiology, bias also means systematic error from the study itself: confounding, selection bias and information bias (misclassification, measurement error). More data reduce random error, not bias.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E[\hat{\theta}] - \theta\).

Related: Confounding, Selection bias, Measurement error, Estimator and estimate · Lessons: 4, 9, 12, 13


Binary variable
Describing data
A variable that takes exactly two values, such as asthma yes or no.
Binary variables are usually coded 0 and 1. Their mean is then the proportion of 1s, which for an outcome is the risk or the prevalence. Binary outcomes are modeled with logistic regression or, for risk ratios, with log-binomial or Poisson models with robust standard errors.

Formal definition. \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) with \(P(Y = 1) = \pi\). Then \(E[Y] = \pi\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \pi(1-\pi)\): \(Y\) follows a Bernoulli distribution distribution.


In R:
mean(cohort$asthma)   # the proportion with asthma

Related: Bernoulli distribution, Risk (cumulative incidence), Logistic regression · Lessons: 1, 3, 8


Binomial distribution
Distributions
The number of “successes” in n independent trials, each with the same probability π.

Formal definition. \[P(Y = k) = \binom{n}{k}\pi^k(1 - \pi)^{n-k}, \quad k = 0, \dots, n\] with \(E[Y] = n\pi\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = n\pi(1-\pi)\).


In R:
dbinom(k, size = n, prob = p)

Related: Bernoulli distribution, Poisson distribution · Lessons: 3


BLUP (best linear unbiased predictor)
Multilevel models
The shrunken estimate of a group’s random effect from a mixed model.

In R:
lme4::ranef(fit)

Related: Random effect, Shrinkage · Lessons: 18


Bootstrap
Sampling and estimation
Estimating the uncertainty of an estimate by recomputing it on many resamples of the data.
Each bootstrap sample draws n observations with replacement from the original data. The spread of the recomputed estimates approximates the sampling distribution. For time series or clustered data, resample blocks or clusters, not individual observations.

Formal definition. Draw \(B\) samples \(y^{*(b)}\) from the empirical distribution, compute \(\hat{\theta}^{*(b)}\), and use the percentiles or the SD of \(\{\hat{\theta}^{*(b)}\}\).

Related: Sampling distribution, Standard error (SE) · Lessons: 4, 16


BYM2 model
Spatial
A spatial model that splits area effects into spatially structured and unstructured parts, with a parameter giving the share that is spatial.

Formal definition. \(u_j = \sigma\left(\sqrt{\rho}\, s_j + \sqrt{1-\rho}\, v_j\right)\), with \(s\) a scaled ICAR effect, \(v_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,1)\), and \(\rho \in [0,1]\) the proportion of spatial variance.

Related: Conditional autoregressive (CAR) model, Disease mapping, Hierarchical (multilevel) model · Lessons: 25

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
C

Case-control study
Study designs
A study that compares the past exposure of people with the outcome (cases) and without it (controls).
Efficient for rare outcomes. Because the proportion of cases is set by the design, risks cannot be estimated, but the odds ratio can, and with appropriate control sampling it estimates the rate ratio.
Related: Odds ratio (OR), Cohort study, Case-crossover design · Lessons: 8


Case-crossover design
Time series
A design comparing each case’s exposure on the event day with their own exposure on nearby control days.
Each person serves as their own control, so time-invariant confounders are removed. The time-stratified version (control days on the same weekday in the same month) gives results equivalent to a time-series model.

Formal definition. Analyzed by conditional logistic regression, strata = case × month; estimates the rate ratio.

Related: Time-series study, Case-control study · Lessons: 15


Central limit theorem (CLT)
Sampling and estimation
Averages of many independent values are approximately normally distributed, whatever the distribution of the values themselves.
This is why so many confidence intervals use the normal distribution. It needs a large enough sample, and more of it when the data are skewed.

Formal definition. For i.i.d. \(X_i\) with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)/\sigma \xrightarrow{d} \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1)\) as \(n \to \infty\).

Related: Normal distribution, Sampling distribution · Lessons: 4


Chain
Bayesian computation
One run of an MCMC sampler. Several chains from different starting points are run to check convergence.
Related: R-hat (potential scale reduction factor), Trace plot · Lessons: 21


Chi-square test
Testing and intervals
A test of association between categorical variables, or of how well counts fit expected values.

Formal definition. \(X^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}\), approximately \(\chi^2\) with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom for an \(r \times c\) table.


In R:
chisq.test(table(cohort$parent_smoke, cohort$asthma))

Related: Likelihood ratio test (LRT) · Lessons: 6


Classical measurement error
Measurement error
Error added to the true value, independent of it. It biases slopes toward zero.
A noisy monitor measuring each child’s exposure produces classical error. In Example B, modeled NO₂ includes classical error, so naive estimates of the NO₂ effect are too small.

Formal definition. \(W = X + U\), \(U \perp X\), \(E[U] = 0\). In linear regression, \(\hat{\beta}_W \to \lambda\beta\) with reliability ratio \(\lambda = \mathrm{Var}(X)/(\mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(U))\).

Related: Regression dilution (attenuation bias), Berkson error, Regression calibration · Lessons: 13


Clustering (clustered data)
Multilevel models
When observations come in groups, such as children within schools, whose members resemble each other.
Clustered observations carry less independent information than their number suggests. Ignoring clustering gives standard errors that are too small.
Related: Intraclass correlation (ICC), Random effect, Robust (sandwich) standard errors · Lessons: 18


Cohort study
Study designs
A study that follows people over time, starting from their exposure, and records who develops the outcome.
Cohorts estimate risks, rates and their ratios directly. Example B is a birth cohort. Cohorts can be prospective or use existing records (retrospective), and are vulnerable to loss to follow-up and confounding.
Related: Case-control study, Risk (cumulative incidence), Risk ratio (RR) · Lessons: 1


Collider
Causal inference
A variable caused by two others on a path. Conditioning on it creates a spurious association.
If both NO₂ and a genetic predisposition lead to a hospital visit, studying only hospitalized children can make NO₂ and the predisposition look related. See collider bias.
Related: Collider bias, Directed acyclic graph (DAG), Selection bias · Lessons: 9


Collider bias
Causal inference
Bias from conditioning on a collider, by adjustment, stratification or selection.
Related: Collider, Selection bias · Lessons: 9, 12


Comparative risk assessment (CRA)
Disease burden
A framework for estimating the burden attributable to risk factors by combining exposure distributions, exposure–response functions and a counterfactual.
The ingredients are an exposure distribution, a relative risk function, a counterfactual exposure (counterfactual exposure), and baseline burden. Uncertainty in each should be propagated, usually by Monte Carlo simulation.
Related: Population attributable fraction (PAF), Counterfactual exposure (TMREL), Disability-adjusted life year (DALY), Exposure–response function (ERF) · Lessons: 14


Conditional autoregressive (CAR) model
Spatial
A model for spatially structured area effects, in which each area’s effect is centered on the average of its neighbors.

Formal definition. Intrinsic CAR: \(u_j \mid u_{-j} \sim \mathrm{Normal}\!\left(\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{k \sim j} u_k,\ \frac{\tau^2}{n_j}\right)\), with \(n_j\) neighbors.

Related: BYM2 model, Neighbors and spatial weights, Disease mapping · Lessons: 25


Conditional probability
Probability
The probability of one event given that another has occurred, written P(A | B).
Conditioning restricts attention to cases where B is true. P(positive test | asthma) and P(asthma | positive test) are different numbers, and confusing them is one of the most common errors in medicine and statistics.

Formal definition. \[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \quad P(B) > 0\]


Don’t confuse. \(P(A \mid B) \neq P(B \mid A)\) in general. A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data).

Related: Bayes’ theorem, Sensitivity, Positive predictive value (PPV), p-value · Lessons: 2


Confidence interval (CI)
Testing and intervals
A range computed by a procedure that, across repeated studies, contains the true value a stated proportion of the time.
A 95% CI comes from a method with 95% coverage. Any single interval either contains the truth or does not. The width shows precision; it says nothing about bias.

Formal definition. An interval \([L(Y), U(Y)]\) with \(P_\theta(L(Y) \le \theta \le U(Y)) = 0.95\) for all \(\theta\). The Wald interval is \(\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96\,SE(\hat{\theta})\).


Don’t confuse. “95% probability that the true value lies in this interval” describes a credible interval, not a confidence interval.


How it’s reported. “RR 1.21 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.38)”

Related: Coverage, Standard error (SE), Credible interval · Lessons: 6


Confounder
Causal inference
A variable that causes, or shares a cause with, both the exposure and the outcome, and is not on the causal path between them.
The classic three criteria (associated with exposure, associated with outcome, not a mediator) are necessary but not sufficient. A directed acyclic graph decides what needs adjusting for.
Related: Confounding, Mediator, Collider, Directed acyclic graph (DAG) · Lessons: 9


Confounding
Causal inference
Distortion of an exposure–outcome association by a third factor that causes both.
In Example B, deprived districts have more traffic (so more NO₂) and children with more asthma risk factors. Part of the crude NO₂–asthma association reflects socio-economic position. In DAG terms, confounding is an open backdoor path.

Formal definition. In potential-outcome terms, confounding means the exposed and unexposed are not exchangeable: \(Y^{x} \not\perp\!\!\!\perp X\), so \(E[Y \mid X = x] \ne E[Y^x]\).


In epidemiology. Controlled by design (randomization, restriction, matching) or analysis (stratification, regression, standardization, propensity scores).

Related: Confounder, Directed acyclic graph (DAG), Backdoor path, Exchangeability, Residual confounding · Lessons: 9, 12


Conjugate prior
Bayesian basics
A prior that, combined with a given likelihood, gives a posterior in the same family.

Formal definition. Poisson–gamma: \(\lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(a, b)\) and \(y_1, \dots, y_n \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\) give \(\lambda \mid y \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(a + \sum y_i,\ b + n)\). Beta–binomial is the analogue for proportions.

Related: Gamma distribution, Beta distribution, Prior distribution · Lessons: 19


Consistency (causal)
Causal inference
The observed outcome of a person equals their potential outcome under the exposure they actually had.
It requires the exposure to be well defined. “Living with high NO₂” can arise in many ways (a busy road, a gas cooker), which may not have the same effect.

Formal definition. If \(X_i = x\) then \(Y_i = Y_i^x\).


Don’t confuse. Unrelated to the statistical meaning of a consistent estimator (one that converges to the truth as n grows).

Related: Potential outcomes, Target trial emulation · Lessons: 12


Continuous variable
Describing data
A measurement that can take any value on a scale, such as temperature or NO₂ concentration.
Differences between values are meaningful, so means and standard deviations make sense. Continuous exposures are best kept continuous in analysis. Dichotomizing them loses information.

Formal definition. A variable taking values in an interval of the real line, \(X \in (a, b) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), described by a probability density.

Related: Dichotomization, Probability density function (PDF) · Lessons: 1


Count variable
Describing data
A variable recording a whole number of events, such as emergency visits per day.
Counts are non-negative integers. Their variance usually grows with their mean, so they are modeled with the Poisson distribution or the negative binomial distribution distribution, typically through Poisson regression.

Formal definition. \(Y \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\). Under a Poisson model, \(E[Y] = \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu\).

Related: Poisson distribution, Overdispersion, Poisson regression · Lessons: 1, 3, 8


Counterfactual exposure (TMREL)
Disease burden
The exposure level that burden is compared against: the attributable cases are those that would not occur at this level.
The theoretical minimum risk exposure level is the lowest level considered achievable or biologically relevant. Choosing zero NO₂ versus a guideline value of 10 µg/m³ can change the attributable burden more than any statistical choice.
Related: Population attributable fraction (PAF), Comparative risk assessment (CRA) · Lessons: 14


Coverage
Testing and intervals
The proportion of intervals, across repeated studies, that contain the true value.
A well-behaved 95% CI has 95% coverage. Intervals that ignore overdispersion, autocorrelation or clustering cover the truth less often than they claim.
Related: Confidence interval (CI) · Lessons: 6


Credible interval
Bayesian basics
An interval containing a stated probability of the posterior, such as 95%.
A 95% credible interval can be read as “given the model, prior and data, there is a 95% probability the parameter lies here”, the reading people often wrongly give to confidence intervals.

Formal definition. Equal-tailed: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of \(p(\theta \mid y)\). Highest density interval: the narrowest region containing 95%.


How it’s reported. “RR 1.14 (95% credible interval 1.03 to 1.26)”

Related: Confidence interval (CI), Posterior distribution · Lessons: 19


Cross-basis
Lags and DLNMs
The set of variables that describes an exposure’s effect jointly over its level and its lag in a DLNM.
Related: Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), Spline · Lessons: 16


Cross-sectional study
Study designs
A study that measures exposure and outcome at the same time.
Cross-sectional studies estimate prevalence. Because exposure and outcome are measured together, they often cannot show which came first.
Related: Prevalence, Cohort study · Lessons: 1


Cross-validation
Model building
Assessing a model by fitting it on part of the data and testing its predictions on the rest.
In k-fold cross-validation, the data are split into k parts and each takes a turn as the test set. For time series, the test set must come after the training set, or blocks must be used.
Related: Overfitting, Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO, PSIS-LOO) · Lessons: 10, 23


Crude and adjusted estimates
Epidemiological measures
A crude estimate ignores other variables. An adjusted estimate accounts for them, usually to remove confounding.
Comparing crude and adjusted estimates shows how much the adjustment variables changed the picture. A large change suggests confounding, but the right adjustment set comes from causal reasoning (directed acyclic graph), not from watching estimates move.

Formal definition. Crude: \(E[Y \mid X]\). Adjusted (conditional): \(E[Y \mid X, Z]\), estimated by including \(Z\) in the regression model or by standardization.


In epidemiology. aOR, aRR and aHR denote adjusted odds, risk and hazard ratios.

Related: Adjusted odds ratio (aOR), Confounding, Adjustment set · Lessons: 1, 9


Crude rate
Standardization
A rate for a whole population without adjustment for its age structure.
The crude rate mixes two things: the age-specific rates and the population’s age structure. A district with many older residents has a high crude rate even if every age group there does as well as elsewhere.

Formal definition. \[\text{crude}_j = \frac{\sum_k D_{jk}}{\sum_k PT_{jk}} = \sum_k \frac{PT_{jk}}{PT_j} r_{jk}\] a weighted average of age-specific rates \(r_{jk}\), weighted by district \(j\)’s own age structure.

Related: Age-specific rate, Direct standardization (age-standardized rate, ASR) · Lessons: 1


Cumulative distribution function (CDF)
Probability
The probability that a random variable is at most a given value.

Formal definition. \(F(x) = P(X \le x)\). For continuous variables, \(F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(u)\,du\).


In R:
pnorm(1.96)   # 0.975

Related: Probability density function (PDF), Quantile (percentile, quartile) · Lessons: 3


Cumulative effect
Lags and DLNMs
The total effect of an exposure summed over all lags.

Formal definition. \(\log RR_{\text{cum}}(x) = \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\log RR(x, \ell)\); its variance needs the full covariance of the lag coefficients.

Related: Distributed lag model (DLM), Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), Harvesting (mortality displacement) · Lessons: 16

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
D

Degrees of freedom (df)
Nonlinear effects
The number of independent pieces of information a quantity uses; for splines, a measure of flexibility.
In time-series studies, “7 df per year” for the time spline sets how much seasonal and long-term variation is absorbed. For penalized splines, the effective df is estimated from the data.
Related: Spline, Penalized spline · Lessons: 11, 15


Deviance
Regression
A measure of lack of fit for GLMs: twice the gap in log-likelihood between a perfect model and yours.

Formal definition. \(D = 2[\ell(\text{saturated}) - \ell(\hat{\beta})]\). Differences in deviance between nested models give the likelihood ratio test.

Related: Log-likelihood, Likelihood ratio test (LRT) · Lessons: 8, 10


Diagnostic likelihood ratio (LR+, LR−)
Diagnostic accuracy
How many times more likely a test result is in people with the condition than without it.
Likelihood ratios update the odds of disease: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR. Not to be confused with the likelihood ratio test.

Formal definition. \(LR^+ = Se/(1 - Sp)\) and \(LR^- = (1 - Se)/Sp\).

Related: Sensitivity, Specificity, Bayes’ theorem · Lessons: 2


Dichotomization
Describing data
Splitting a continuous variable into two groups at a cut-off.
Dichotomizing throws away information, reduces power, and makes results depend on an arbitrary cut-off. Children just above and just below 30 µg/m³ are treated as completely different, while children at 31 and 60 µg/m³ are treated as the same. Prefer keeping the variable continuous, with splines if the relation is not linear.

In epidemiology. Common in older papers (“high vs low exposure”). When cut-offs are chosen after looking at the data, the results are biased toward finding an effect.

Related: Continuous variable, Spline · Lessons: 1, 11


Differential misclassification
Measurement error
Misclassification whose rates differ between the groups compared, which can bias in either direction.
Parents of children with asthma may report past exposures differently (recall bias).
Related: Non-differential misclassification, Misclassification · Lessons: 13


Direct standardization (age-standardized rate, ASR)
Standardization
Applying each population’s age-specific rates to a common standard age structure, so rates can be compared without age differences.
The age-standardized rate answers: what would this population’s rate be if it had the age structure of the standard? It requires age-specific rates in each population, which can be unstable for small populations; then indirect standardization is used.

Formal definition. \[ASR_j = \sum_k w_k\, r_{jk}, \qquad w_k = \frac{N_k^{\mathrm{std}}}{\sum_{k'} N_{k'}^{\mathrm{std}}}\]


In epidemiology. Common standards include the WHO world standard population and the European standard population. Standardized rates are only comparable when they use the same standard.


In R:
age_rates |> left_join(std_w, by = "age_group") |> group_by(district) |> summarise(asr = sum(w * r))


How it’s reported. “age-standardized rate 236 per 1,000 person-years (direct method, city standard population)”

Related: Crude rate, Standard population, Indirect standardization, Standardized morbidity or mortality ratio (SMR) · Lessons: 1


Directed acyclic graph (DAG)
Causal inference
A diagram of assumed causal relations, with arrows from causes to effects and no loops.
A DAG makes your assumptions explicit and tells you which variables to adjust for (an adjustment set) to block confounding without opening bias through colliders or mediators.

Formal definition. A graph \(G = (V, E)\) of variables and directed edges with no directed cycles. The backdoor criterion identifies \(E[Y^x]\) when a set \(Z\) blocks every path from \(X\) to \(Y\) that starts with an arrow into \(X\), and \(Z\) contains no descendant of \(X\).


In R:
dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "no2", outcome = "asthma")

Related: Backdoor path, Adjustment set, Confounder, Collider · Lessons: 9, 12


Dirichlet process prior
Hierarchical models
A semiparametric prior that lets coefficients cluster into an unknown number of groups with shared values.
Used for many correlated exposures: instead of one bell curve, the coefficients may form several clusters, one of which can sit at zero (variable selection).

Formal definition. \(\beta_j \sim G\), \(G \sim \mathrm{DP}(\alpha, G_0)\); draws from \(G\) are discrete, so coefficients tie.

Related: Hierarchical (multilevel) model, Shrinkage · Lessons: 24


Disability weight
Disease burden
A number between 0 (full health) and 1 (equivalent to death) expressing the severity of a health state.
Disability weights come from population surveys in which people compare health states. They are a value judgment as much as a measurement.
Related: Years lived with disability (YLD), Disability-adjusted life year (DALY) · Lessons: 14


Disability-adjusted life year (DALY)
Disease burden
A measure of disease burden that adds years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability.
One DALY is one lost year of healthy life. DALYs let burden be compared across diseases that kill and diseases that disable, such as childhood asthma, which mostly contributes years lived with disability.

Formal definition. \(DALY = YLL + YLD\).


In epidemiology. Used by the Global Burden of Disease study. Results depend on the disability weights, the reference life table and, in older versions, on age weighting and discounting.

Related: Years of life lost (YLL), Years lived with disability (YLD), Disability weight, Population attributable fraction (PAF) · Lessons: 14


Disease mapping
Spatial
Mapping area-level disease risk, usually as smoothed relative risks or SMRs.

Formal definition. \(O_j \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(E_j\theta_j)\), \(\log\theta_j = \alpha + u_j + v_j\), with spatially structured \(u_j\) and unstructured \(v_j\) effects.

Related: Standardized morbidity or mortality ratio (SMR), BYM2 model, Conditional autoregressive (CAR) model · Lessons: 17, 25


Distributed lag model (DLM)
Lags and DLNMs
A model in which the effect of an exposure is spread over several days, with one coefficient per lag.
Unconstrained DLMs have highly correlated lag coefficients (multicollinearity) and noisy estimates. Constraining the lag curve to a smooth shape stabilizes them.

Formal definition. \(\log\mu_t = \alpha + \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\beta_\ell\, x_{t-\ell} + \dots\), with cumulative effect \(\sum_\ell \beta_\ell\).

Related: Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), Lag, Cumulative effect, Multicollinearity · Lessons: 16


Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM)
Lags and DLNMs
A model that lets an exposure’s effect be non-linear in its level and spread over several lags at once.
The effect is a surface over exposure level and lag, built from a cross-basis. Summaries include the cumulative exposure–response function, the minimum morbidity or mortality temperature, and relative risks at chosen percentiles.

Formal definition. \(\log\mu_t = \alpha + \sum_{j}\sum_{k} \eta_{jk}\, w_{t,jk} + \dots\), where \(w_{t,jk} = \sum_\ell b_j(x_{t-\ell})\, c_k(\ell)\) combine a basis \(b_j\) in the exposure and \(c_k\) in the lag.


In R:
cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(d$temp, lag = 21,
                       argvar = list(fun = "ns", df = 4), arglag = list(fun = "ns", df = 4))


How it’s reported. “RR at the 99th temperature percentile relative to the MMT: 1.32 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.48), cumulative over lags 0–21”

Related: Cross-basis, Exposure–response function (ERF), Minimum morbidity or mortality temperature (MMT), Lag–response curve · Lessons: 16


Divergent transition
Bayesian computation
A warning from Stan that the sampler could not explore part of the posterior reliably.
Divergences often signal a difficult geometry, such as the funnel in hierarchical models. Do not ignore them; reparameterize or rethink the priors.
Related: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC, NUTS), Non-centered parameterization (funnel) · Lessons: 21, 24

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
E

E-value
Causal inference
The minimum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome to explain away an observed effect.

Formal definition. For an observed \(RR > 1\): \(E = RR + \sqrt{RR(RR - 1)}\).


In R:
EValue::evalues.RR(est = 1.21, lo = 1.06, hi = 1.38)

Related: Residual confounding, Quantitative bias analysis · Lessons: 12


Ecological fallacy
Spatial
Wrongly concluding that an association between area averages holds for the individuals within them.
Related: Ecological study, Areal data · Lessons: 17


Ecological study
Study designs
A study whose units are groups, such as districts, rather than individuals.
Associations between group averages need not hold for individuals (ecological fallacy). Time-series studies of daily counts are ecological in a sense, but they compare the same population with itself over time, which limits confounding.
Related: Ecological fallacy, Time-series study · Lessons: 17


Effect modification
Causal inference
When the effect of an exposure differs across levels of another variable.
Heat harms older people more than younger: age modifies the heat effect. Effect modification depends on the scale: an effect can be constant on the ratio scale but differ on the difference scale (additive and multiplicative interaction).

In epidemiology. Assess it by comparing stratum-specific estimates with a formal test or interval for their difference, never by comparing their p-values.


Don’t confuse. “Significant in the elderly, not significant in the young” is not evidence of effect modification.

Related: Interaction, Additive and multiplicative interaction (RERI), Heterogeneity · Lessons: 9, 23


Effective sample size (ESS)
Bayesian computation
The number of independent draws that would carry the same information as the correlated MCMC draws.

Formal definition. \(ESS = \frac{N}{1 + 2\sum_{k \ge 1}\rho_k}\), with \(\rho_k\) the autocorrelation of the chain at lag \(k\).

Related: R-hat (potential scale reduction factor), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) · Lessons: 21


Equivalence test (TOST)
Testing and intervals
A test designed to support “the effect is negligibly small”, using a margin set in advance.
Two one-sided tests check whether the effect is above −δ and below +δ. Both must reject. It is the frequentist way to provide evidence for the absence of a meaningful effect.

Formal definition. Test \(H_0: |\theta| \ge \delta\) against \(H_1: |\theta| < \delta\), rejecting when both one-sided p-values are below α; equivalently, when the \((1-2\alpha)\) CI lies inside \((-\delta, \delta)\).

Related: Null hypothesis (H0), Region of practical equivalence (ROPE) · Lessons: 6, 23


Estimator and estimate
Sampling and estimation
An estimator is a rule for computing a guess of a parameter from data. An estimate is the number it produces.
The sample mean is an estimator; 436 visits per day is an estimate. Estimators are judged by their bias, their variance, and their combination, the mean squared error.

Formal definition. An estimator is a function of the data, \(\hat{\theta} = g(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)\), itself a random variable with a sampling distribution. \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Bias}^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})\).

Related: Bias, Sampling distribution, Standard error (SE) · Lessons: 4


Exchangeability
Causal inference
In causal inference: the exposed and unexposed would have had the same outcome risk had they had the same exposure. In Bayesian modeling: units whose labels carry no information.
Causal exchangeability means no confounding, possibly after conditioning on covariates. Randomization guarantees it on average. In hierarchical models, exchangeability of districts justifies giving them a common prior distribution.

Formal definition. Causal: \(Y^x \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Z\) for all \(x\). Bayesian: the joint distribution of \((\theta_1, \dots, \theta_J)\) is invariant to permuting the indices.

Related: Confounding, Potential outcomes, Hierarchical (multilevel) model · Lessons: 12, 24


Expected value
Probability
The long-run average value of a random variable, weighting each value by its probability.

Formal definition. \(E[X] = \sum_x x\,p(x)\) (discrete) or \(E[X] = \int x\,f(x)\,dx\) (continuous). Expectation is linear: \(E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]\).

Related: Mean, Variance, Random variable · Lessons: 3


Exposure–response function (ERF)
Lags and DLNMs
The curve showing how the relative risk changes across exposure levels.
For temperature it is typically U- or J-shaped, with a minimum at the minimum morbidity or mortality temperature. In a DLNM it is usually reported cumulatively over all lags.
Related: Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), Minimum morbidity or mortality temperature (MMT), Cumulative effect · Lessons: 11, 16

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
F

Fisher information
Likelihood
How sharply the likelihood peaks: more information means a smaller standard error.

Formal definition. \(I(\theta) = -E\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta^2}\right]\), with \(SE(\hat{\theta}) \approx 1/\sqrt{I(\hat{\theta})}\). The observed information uses the curvature at the MLE without the expectation.

Related: Maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), Standard error (SE) · Lessons: 5


Fixed effect
Multilevel models
An effect treated as a fixed unknown constant, estimated separately for each group without borrowing information across groups.

Don’t confuse. “Fixed effects” means different things in econometrics, in mixed models and in meta-analysis. Check which is meant.

Related: Random effect, Partial pooling (no pooling, complete pooling) · Lessons: 18


Fourier terms
Time series
Sine and cosine terms used to model smooth seasonal cycles.

Formal definition. \(\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left[a_h \sin\left(\frac{2\pi h\, t}{365.25}\right) + b_h \cos\left(\frac{2\pi h\, t}{365.25}\right)\right]\).

Related: Seasonality · Lessons: 15

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
G

G-computation (standardization)
Causal inference
Estimating a causal effect by predicting everyone’s outcome under each exposure level and averaging the predictions.
Fit an outcome model, set everyone’s exposure to high, predict, average; set it to low, predict, average; then compare. It turns a conditional model into a marginal effect such as a risk ratio, even from logistic regression.

Formal definition. \(\widehat{E}[Y^x] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \widehat{E}[Y \mid X = x, Z = z_i]\).


In R:
fit <- glm(asthma ~ high_no2 + ses + parent_smoke, family = binomial, data = cohort)
mean(predict(fit, mutate(cohort, high_no2 = TRUE), type = "response")) /
  mean(predict(fit, mutate(cohort, high_no2 = FALSE), type = "response"))

Related: Average causal effect (ATE), Inverse probability weighting (IPW), Marginal and conditional effects · Lessons: 12


Gamma distribution
Distributions
A flexible distribution for positive quantities, often used as a prior for rates.

Formal definition. \(f(x) = \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)} x^{a-1} e^{-bx}\), \(x > 0\), with mean \(a/b\) and variance \(a/b^2\). It is the conjugate prior for a Poisson rate.

Related: Conjugate prior, Negative binomial distribution · Lessons: 19


Generalized additive model (GAM)
Nonlinear effects
A GLM in which some predictors enter through smooth functions estimated from the data.

Formal definition. \(g(\mu_i) = \alpha + f_1(x_{1i}) + f_2(x_{2i}) + z_i^\top\gamma\), with each \(f_j\) a penalized spline.


In R:
mgcv::gam(visits ~ s(temp) + s(doy, bs = "cc"), family = quasipoisson, data = d)

Related: Penalized spline, Generalized linear model (GLM) · Lessons: 11


Generalized linear model (GLM)
Regression
A regression model made of a distribution for the outcome, a link function, and a linear predictor.
Logistic regression (binomial distribution, logit link) and Poisson regression (Poisson distribution, log link) are GLMs. Linear regression is the special case with a normal distribution and identity link.

Formal definition. \[Y_i \sim \text{exponential family}(\mu_i), \quad g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = x_i^\top\beta\] where \(g\) is the link function and \(\eta_i\) the linear predictor.


In R:
glm(y ~ x, family = poisson(link = "log"), data = d)

Related: Link function, Logistic regression, Poisson regression · Lessons: 8


Grid approximation
Bayesian computation
Computing a posterior by evaluating prior × likelihood on a grid of parameter values.
Works for one or two parameters, which is why it is used for teaching. With many parameters the grid becomes impossibly large, and MCMC is used instead.
Related: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), Posterior distribution · Lessons: 19

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
H

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC, NUTS)
Bayesian computation
An MCMC algorithm that uses the shape of the posterior to make long, efficient moves. Stan uses it.
Related: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), Divergent transition · Lessons: 21


Harvesting (mortality displacement)
Time series
When an exposure brings forward events by only a few days among people who were already very frail.
Shows as an excess followed by a deficit in the lag–response curve. The cumulative effect over a long enough lag accounts for it.
Related: Lag, Distributed lag model (DLM), Cumulative effect · Lessons: 16


Hazard ratio (HR)
Epidemiological measures
The ratio of instantaneous event rates between two groups, from survival analysis.
Hazard ratios come from Cox proportional hazards models. They resemble rate ratios and are interpreted similarly, but they compare event rates at each moment among those still at risk. This course does not cover survival analysis, but you will meet HRs in cohort papers.

Formal definition. \(HR = h_1(t)/h_0(t)\), assumed constant over time under proportional hazards, where \(h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} P(t \le T < t + \Delta t \mid T \ge t)/\Delta t\).

Related: Rate ratio (incidence rate ratio, IRR), Risk ratio (RR)


Heterogeneity
Multilevel models
Genuine variation in effects between studies, places or groups, beyond what chance explains.
Heat effects differ between cities and districts because of climate, housing and population. In meta-analysis it is quantified by τ² (the variance of true effects) and I² (the share of observed variation due to real differences). Explaining it is the job of meta-regression and effect modification analyses.

Formal definition. Cochran’s \(Q = \sum_k w_k(\hat{\theta}_k - \hat{\theta})^2\) with \(w_k = 1/s_k^2\); \(I^2 = \max\left(0, \frac{Q - (K-1)}{Q}\right)\); \(\tau^2 = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_k)\).


Don’t confuse. Not the same as heteroskedasticity, which is non-constant error variance within a single model.

Related: Meta-analysis, Effect modification, Heteroskedasticity, Random slope · Lessons: 18, 24


Heteroskedasticity
Regression
Error variance that changes with the predictors or the fitted values.
Coefficient estimates remain unbiased, but standard errors are wrong. It shows as a funnel in a plot of residuals against fitted values. Remedies: model the variance (GLMs), transform the outcome, or use robust standard errors.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid x_i) = \sigma_i^2\), not constant. Not to be confused with heterogeneity, which concerns effects, not error variance.


Don’t confuse. Heteroskedasticity is about unequal error variance within one model. Heterogeneity is about different effects across studies, groups or places.

Related: Homoskedasticity, Robust (sandwich) standard errors, Heterogeneity · Lessons: 7, 8


Hierarchical (multilevel) model
Hierarchical models
A model in which group-level parameters are themselves given a distribution with its own unknown parameters, so groups inform each other.
District heat effects, school effects or exposure-specific coefficients are drawn from a common distribution whose mean and spread are learned from the data. This produces partial pooling and stabilizes estimates for small groups and correlated exposures.

Formal definition. \(y_{ij} \sim p(y \mid \theta_j)\), \(\theta_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \tau^2)\), with hyperpriors \(p(\mu)\), \(p(\tau)\).


In R:
brms::brm(visits ~ temp + (1 + temp | district), family = negbinomial, data = d)

Related: Hyperprior, Partial pooling (no pooling, complete pooling), Random effect, Exchangeability · Lessons: 24, 25


Histogram
Describing data
A chart that shows a distribution by counting values that fall in adjacent intervals (bins).
The height of each bar is the number (or proportion) of observations in that bin. The shape reveals skewness, several peaks, or outliers. The impression depends on the bin width, so try more than one.

In R:
ggplot(city_daily, aes(pm25)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)

Related: Skewness, Outlier · Lessons: 1


Homoskedasticity
Regression
Constant variance of the errors across all values of the predictors.
An assumption of standard linear regression. Counts usually violate it, because their variance grows with their mean, which is one reason to use Poisson or negative binomial models.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid x_i) = \sigma^2\) for all \(i\).

Related: Heteroskedasticity, Linear regression · Lessons: 7


Hyperprior
Hierarchical models
A prior on the parameters of a prior, such as the between-district standard deviation τ.
Hyperpriors on variance parameters matter. Half-normal or exponential priors on τ are safer than the once-common inverse-gamma(0.001, 0.001).

Formal definition. E.g. \(\tau \sim \mathrm{Half\text{-}Normal}(0, 0.1)\) in \(\theta_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \tau^2)\).

Related: Hierarchical (multilevel) model, Prior distribution · Lessons: 24

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
I

Incidence rate
Epidemiological measures
The number of events per unit of person-time, such as visits per 1,000 person-years.
Rates are used when people can have repeated events, or are observed for different lengths of time. The denominator is the total person-time at risk. A rate has units (per year) and can exceed 1.

Formal definition. \(I = D / PT\), an estimate of the hazard averaged over the period. Under a Poisson model the number of events is \(D \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(I \cdot PT)\).


In epidemiology. Also called incidence density. Emergency visit rates in Example A are rates of (possibly repeated) events, not risks.


In R:
visits |> summarise(rate = 1000 * sum(visits) / (sum(population) / 365.25))


How it’s reported. “240 emergency visits per 1,000 person-years”

Related: Person-time, Rate ratio (incidence rate ratio, IRR), Risk (cumulative incidence), Poisson regression · Lessons: 1, 8


Independence
Probability
Two events or variables are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
Many methods assume independent observations. Daily counts are not independent over time (autocorrelation), children in the same school are not independent (clustering), and neighboring districts are not independent (spatial autocorrelation). Ignoring this makes standard errors too small.

Formal definition. Events: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), equivalently \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\). Random variables: the joint distribution factorizes, \(f(x, y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y)\).

Related: Conditional probability, Autocorrelation, Clustering (clustered data) · Lessons: 2, 15, 18


Indirect standardization
Standardization
Applying standard age-specific rates to a population’s age structure to get the number of expected events, then comparing observed with expected.
Used when a population is too small for reliable age-specific rates. The result is the standardized morbidity or mortality ratio, observed divided by expected. Indirect standardization is the basis of disease mapping in Lesson 17.

Formal definition. \(E_j = \sum_k r_k^{\mathrm{std}}\, PT_{jk}\) and \(SMR_j = O_j / E_j\).

Related: Standardized morbidity or mortality ratio (SMR), Direct standardization (age-standardized rate, ASR), Disease mapping · Lessons: 1, 17


Influential observation (Cook’s distance)
Model building
An observation whose removal would change the fitted model substantially.
Influence combines an unusual outcome (a large residual) with an unusual predictor value (high leverage). A single extreme heat-wave day can be influential in a temperature model.

Formal definition. \(D_i = \frac{\sum_j(\hat{y}_j - \hat{y}_{j(i)})^2}{p\,\hat{\sigma}^2}\), where \(\hat{y}_{j(i)}\) is the fit without observation \(i\).


In R:
cooks.distance(fit)

Related: Leverage, Outlier, Residual · Lessons: 10


Informative (order-constrained) hypothesis
Bayesian model comparison
A hypothesis stated as constraints on several parameters, such as “harmful in the elderly and larger than in the young”.

Formal definition. Encompassing-prior Bayes factor against the unconstrained model: \(BF_{iu} = f_i / c_i\), the share of posterior draws satisfying the constraints divided by the share of prior draws satisfying them.


In R:
bain::bain(fit, "b_old > b_young > 0")

Related: Bayes factor, Effect modification · Lessons: 23


Informative prior
Priors
A prior that encodes substantial existing knowledge, such as results of earlier studies.
Related: Weakly informative prior, Vague (non-informative) prior, Prior distribution · Lessons: 20


INLA (integrated nested Laplace approximation)
Bayesian computation
A fast, accurate approximation to Bayesian posteriors for a large class of hierarchical models, widely used for spatial and spatio-temporal models.
Related: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), BYM2 model, Hierarchical (multilevel) model · Lessons: 25


Interaction
Causal inference
A model term that lets the effect of one variable depend on the value of another.

Formal definition. \(g(\mu) = \alpha + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 z + \beta_3 xz\). The effect of \(x\) is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 z\), and \(H_0: \beta_3 = 0\) tests for interaction on the scale of the link.


In R:
glm(visits ~ temp * age_group, family = quasipoisson, data = visits)

Related: Effect modification, Additive and multiplicative interaction (RERI) · Lessons: 9


Intercept
Regression
The model’s prediction when all predictors equal zero. Often written α.
It is meaningful only if zero is a sensible value for every predictor, which is why predictors are often centered (temperature − 20°C).
Related: Regression coefficient, Slope · Lessons: 7


Interquartile range (IQR)
Describing data
The range covered by the middle 50% of values, from the first to the third quartile.
The IQR is robust to extreme values, so it pairs with the median for skewed data. In publications it is usually reported as the two quartiles, “Q1–Q3”, rather than their difference. Air pollution effects are sometimes expressed “per IQR increase” in exposure.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{IQR} = Q(0.75) - Q(0.25)\).


In R:
IQR(x); quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75))


How it’s reported. “median 12.4 (IQR 9.8–15.9)”

Related: Median, Quantile (percentile, quartile), Standard deviation (SD) · Lessons: 1


Intraclass correlation (ICC)
Multilevel models
The share of the total variation that lies between clusters, or the correlation between two members of the same cluster.

Formal definition. \(ICC = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2}\); for logistic models, \(\sigma^2 = \pi^2/3\) on the latent scale. Design effect \(= 1 + (m - 1)\,ICC\) for clusters of size \(m\).

Related: Clustering (clustered data), Random intercept · Lessons: 18


Inverse probability weighting (IPW)
Causal inference
Weighting each person by the inverse of the probability of the exposure they received, to create a pseudo-population without confounding.

Formal definition. Weights \(w_i = 1/e(z_i)\) for the exposed and \(1/(1 - e(z_i))\) for the unexposed, then \(\widehat{E}[Y^1] = \sum_i w_i X_i Y_i / \sum_i w_i X_i\). Stabilized weights multiply by \(P(X = x)\).


In R:
WeightIt::weightit(high_no2 ~ ses + parent_smoke + green, data = cohort)

Related: Propensity score, G-computation (standardization) · Lessons: 12

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
K

Knot
Nonlinear effects
A point where the pieces of a spline join.
More knots give more flexibility. They are usually placed at quantiles of the variable. Choosing knots after looking at which gives the most striking result is a form of data dredging.
Related: Spline, Degrees of freedom (df) · Lessons: 11


Kriging
Spatial
Spatial interpolation that predicts values at unmeasured locations from nearby measurements, weighted by their spatial correlation.
Related: Point-referenced data, Spatial autocorrelation · Lessons: 17

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
L

Lag
Lags and DLNMs
The delay between an exposure and its effect: lag 2 means the exposure two days earlier.

Formal definition. The exposure at lag \(\ell\) for day \(t\) is \(x_{t-\ell}\).

Related: Distributed lag model (DLM), Lag–response curve, Harvesting (mortality displacement) · Lessons: 15, 16


Lag–response curve
Lags and DLNMs
The curve showing how the effect of an exposure at a given level is distributed over lags.
Related: Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), Lag, Harvesting (mortality displacement) · Lessons: 16


Land-use regression (LUR)
Measurement error
A model that predicts air pollution at any address from nearby traffic, land use and other geographic predictors, calibrated on monitoring data.
The predictions are smoother than true exposure, which mixes classical and Berkson-type errors.
Related: Measurement error, Berkson error · Lessons: 13


Laplace approximation
Bayesian computation
Approximating a posterior or an integral by a normal distribution centered at its peak.

Formal definition. \(\log p(y) \approx \log p(y \mid \hat{\theta}) + \log p(\hat{\theta}) + \frac{k}{2}\log 2\pi - \frac{1}{2}\log|H|\), with \(H\) the negative Hessian of the log posterior at its mode \(\hat{\theta}\).

Related: INLA (integrated nested Laplace approximation), Marginal likelihood (evidence) · Lessons: 23, 25


Least squares (OLS)
Regression
Estimating a regression by choosing the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals.

Formal definition. \(\hat{\beta} = \arg\min_\beta \sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\). With normal errors, this is also the maximum likelihood estimate.

Related: Linear regression, Residual, Maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) · Lessons: 7


Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO, PSIS-LOO)
Bayesian model comparison
Comparing Bayesian models by how well each predicts every observation when that observation is left out.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{elpd}_{\text{loo}} = \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid y_{-i})\), estimated by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling without refitting.


In R:
loo::loo_compare(loo(fit1), loo(fit2))

Related: Widely applicable information criterion (WAIC), Cross-validation, Akaike information criterion (AIC) · Lessons: 23


Leverage
Model building
How unusual an observation’s predictor values are, and so how strongly it can pull the fit.

Formal definition. The diagonal element \(h_{ii}\) of the hat matrix \(H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\).

Related: Influential observation (Cook’s distance) · Lessons: 10


Likelihood
Likelihood
How probable the observed data are under each possible value of the parameters, viewed as a function of the parameters.
The likelihood is the model equation plus its distribution, evaluated on the data. It is the shared engine of frequentist and Bayesian inference: maximum likelihood finds its peak, and Bayesian inference multiplies it by the prior.

Formal definition. \(L(\theta) = p(y \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(y_i \mid \theta)\) for independent observations. It is not a probability distribution over \(\theta\).


Don’t confuse. The likelihood of a parameter value is not the probability that the value is true.

Related: Log-likelihood, Maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), Posterior distribution, Prior distribution · Lessons: 5, 19


Likelihood ratio test (LRT)
Testing and intervals
A test comparing two nested models by how much better the larger one fits.

Formal definition. \(D = 2(\ell_1 - \ell_0)\), approximately \(\chi^2_k\) under the null, where \(k\) is the number of extra parameters in the larger model.


In R:
anova(fit0, fit1, test = "LRT")

Related: Nested models, Deviance, Akaike information criterion (AIC) · Lessons: 10


Lindley’s paradox
Bayesian model comparison
A clearly significant result can come with a Bayes factor favoring the null, when the prior under the alternative is very vague.
A vague alternative spreads its predictions over huge effects that never happen, so it predicts the data poorly. The fix is a prior based on subject knowledge.
Related: Bayes factor, Vague (non-informative) prior, Marginal likelihood (evidence) · Lessons: 23


Linear regression
Regression
A model in which the mean of a continuous outcome is a linear function of the predictors.
Each coefficient is the expected change in the outcome per unit change in a predictor, holding the others fixed. It assumes linearity, independent errors, constant variance (homoskedasticity) and, for small-sample inference, normally distributed errors.

Formal definition. \[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_p x_{pi} + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma^2)\] or in matrix form \(Y = X\beta + \varepsilon\).


In R:
lm(outcome ~ x1 + x2, data = d)

Related: Least squares (OLS), Residual, Generalized linear model (GLM), Homoskedasticity · Lessons: 7


Link function
Regression
The transformation that connects the mean of the outcome to the linear predictor.
The log link keeps expected counts positive and makes effects multiplicative (rate ratios). The logit link keeps probabilities between 0 and 1 and makes effects odds ratios.

Formal definition. \(g(\mu) = \eta\); log link \(g(\mu) = \log\mu\); logit link \(g(\pi) = \log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\).

Related: Generalized linear model (GLM), Logit (log-odds) · Lessons: 8


Log-likelihood
Likelihood
The logarithm of the likelihood, which turns products over observations into sums.

Formal definition. \(\ell(\theta) = \log L(\theta) = \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid \theta)\). Differences in log-likelihood are used in likelihood ratio tests and in Akaike information criterion.

Related: Likelihood, Maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), Deviance · Lessons: 5


Logistic regression
Regression
A GLM for binary outcomes, whose coefficients are log odds ratios.

Formal definition. \[Y_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_i), \quad \mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = \alpha + \beta x_i + \gamma^\top z_i\] so \(e^{\beta}\) is the (adjusted) odds ratio per unit of \(x\).


In R:
glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses, family = binomial, data = cohort)


How it’s reported. “aOR 1.12 per 10 µg/m³ (95% CI 1.01 to 1.24)”

Related: Odds ratio (OR), Adjusted odds ratio (aOR), Logit (log-odds), Generalized linear model (GLM) · Lessons: 8


Logit (log-odds)
Regression
The logarithm of the odds, the scale on which logistic regression is linear.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \log\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}\), with inverse \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}\).

Related: Odds, Logistic regression, Link function · Lessons: 8


Long-term trend
Time series
Slow change in the level of a series over years, from changes in population, coding or services.
Related: Seasonality, Time-series study · Lessons: 15

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
M

Marginal and conditional effects
Causal inference
A marginal effect compares the whole population under different exposures; a conditional effect compares people with the same covariate values.
For risk differences and risk ratios without effect modification they coincide. For odds ratios they generally differ (non-collapsibility).
Related: Non-collapsibility, G-computation (standardization), Adjusted odds ratio (aOR) · Lessons: 12


Marginal likelihood (evidence)
Bayesian model comparison
How well a model predicted the data before seeing it, averaging the likelihood over the prior.
It penalizes models whose priors spread over many values that turn out to be wrong. It is the ingredient of Bayes factors, and is very sensitive to the prior.

Formal definition. \(p(y \mid M) = \int p(y \mid \theta, M)\,p(\theta \mid M)\,d\theta\).


In R:
bridgesampling::bridge_sampler(fit)

Related: Bayes factor, Lindley’s paradox · Lessons: 23


Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
Bayesian computation
Algorithms that draw samples from the posterior by wandering through parameter space, spending time in each region in proportion to its posterior probability.

Formal definition. A Markov chain \(\theta^{(1)}, \theta^{(2)}, \dots\) whose stationary distribution is \(p(\theta \mid y)\); averages over the chain converge to posterior expectations.

Related: Metropolis algorithm, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC, NUTS), R-hat (potential scale reduction factor), Effective sample size (ESS), Posterior draws · Lessons: 21


Maximum likelihood estimate (MLE)
Likelihood
The parameter value that makes the observed data most probable: the peak of the likelihood.
glm() and most standard software find MLEs by iterative algorithms. When the likelihood is flat in some direction, for example with highly correlated exposures, the algorithm may fail to converge.

Formal definition. \(\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta)\), typically solving \(\partial \ell / \partial \theta = 0\). Under regularity conditions \(\hat{\theta} \approx \mathrm{Normal}(\theta, I(\theta)^{-1})\).

Related: Likelihood, Fisher information, Wald test · Lessons: 5


Mean
Describing data
The sum of the values divided by their number. It uses every value, so extreme values pull it.
The mean is the balance point of a distribution. For roughly symmetric data it is the natural summary of a typical value. For skewed data, a long tail drags it away from where most values lie, and the median describes a typical value better.

Formal definition. \[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\] The population mean of a random variable is its expected value, \(E[X]\). The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of it.


Don’t confuse. The mean of the data describes a typical value. The standard error describes how precisely the mean is estimated.


In R:
mean(x)


How it’s reported. Mean (SD), for example “a mean of 436 visits per day (SD 52)”.

Related: Median, Standard deviation (SD), Expected value, Skewness · Lessons: 1, 4


Measurement error
Measurement error
The difference between a measured value and the true value of a variable.
In air pollution epidemiology, exposure is always estimated (from monitors or models), never measured perfectly. The type of error determines the direction of bias: classical measurement error attenuates effects, Berkson error mostly widens intervals.

Formal definition. Measured \(W\) and true \(X\): classical \(W = X + U\); Berkson \(X = W + U\); with \(U\) independent of \(X\) (classical) or of \(W\) (Berkson).

Related: Classical measurement error, Berkson error, Misclassification, Regression dilution (attenuation bias) · Lessons: 13


Median
Describing data
The middle value when the data are ordered: half the values lie below it.
The median ignores how extreme the extremes are, so it is robust to outliers and to long tails. It is the preferred summary of a typical value for skewed data, reported with the interquartile range.

Formal definition. The 0.5 quantile: a value \(m\) such that \(P(X \le m) \ge 0.5\) and \(P(X \ge m) \ge 0.5\). For ordered data \(x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}\), \(m = x_{((n+1)/2)}\) when \(n\) is odd, and the average of the two middle values when \(n\) is even.


In R:
median(x)


How it’s reported. Median (IQR), for example “median PM2.5 12.4 µg/m³ (IQR 9.8–15.9)”.

Related: Mean, Interquartile range (IQR), Quantile (percentile, quartile), Skewness · Lessons: 1


Mediator
Causal inference
A variable on the causal path from exposure to outcome.
Adjusting for a mediator removes part of the effect you want to estimate. Green space may reduce asthma partly by lowering NO₂; if NO₂ is the exposure, green space is a confounder, but if green space is the exposure, NO₂ is a mediator.
Related: Confounder, Collider, Directed acyclic graph (DAG) · Lessons: 9, 12


Meta-analysis
Multilevel models
Combining estimates from several studies or locations into an overall estimate.
Multi-city temperature studies often use a two-stage design: fit a DLNM in each city, then pool the city-specific curves with a multivariate meta-analysis. Random-effects meta-analysis allows true effects to differ (heterogeneity).

Formal definition. Random effects: \(\hat{\theta}_k \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\theta_k, s_k^2)\), \(\theta_k \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \tau^2)\); pooled \(\hat{\mu} = \sum_k w_k\hat{\theta}_k/\sum_k w_k\) with \(w_k = 1/(s_k^2 + \hat{\tau}^2)\).


In R:
mixmeta::mixmeta(coefs ~ 1, S = vcovs, method = "reml")

Related: Heterogeneity, Random effect, Partial pooling (no pooling, complete pooling) · Lessons: 18


Metropolis algorithm
Bayesian computation
An MCMC algorithm that proposes random jumps and always accepts uphill moves, sometimes downhill ones.

Formal definition. Propose \(\theta^* \sim q(\cdot \mid \theta)\) (symmetric); accept with probability \(\min\left(1, \frac{p(\theta^* \mid y)}{p(\theta \mid y)}\right)\).

Related: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC, NUTS) · Lessons: 21


Minimum morbidity or mortality temperature (MMT)
Lags and DLNMs
The temperature at which the cumulative exposure–response curve is lowest, used as the reference for relative risks.
The MMT is itself an estimate with uncertainty, often wide and asymmetric. Conventional intervals for RRs treat it as known, which is why they pinch to zero width at the reference.

Formal definition. \(\mathrm{MMT} = \arg\min_x \log RR_{\text{cum}}(x)\) over a restricted range, often the 1st–99th percentiles.

Related: Exposure–response function (ERF), Distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM) · Lessons: 16, 25


Misclassification
Measurement error
Measurement error in a categorical variable: putting someone in the wrong category.
Described by sensitivity and specificity. The wheeze questionnaire in Example B misclassifies some children’s asthma status.
Related: Non-differential misclassification, Differential misclassification, Sensitivity, Specificity · Lessons: 13


Mode
Describing data
The most frequent value, or the peak of a distribution.
Useful for categorical data and for describing the shape of a distribution. A distribution with two peaks is called bimodal, as daily temperature is (winter and summer).

Formal definition. For a discrete variable, the value \(x\) maximizing \(P(X = x)\). For a continuous variable, the value maximizing the density \(f(x)\).

Related: Mean, Median · Lessons: 1


Moran’s I
Spatial
A statistic measuring spatial autocorrelation: positive when neighbors resemble each other.

Formal definition. \[I = \frac{n}{\sum_{ij} w_{ij}} \frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}(y_i - \bar{y})(y_j - \bar{y})}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}\] with \(E[I] = -1/(n-1)\) under no autocorrelation, usually tested by permutation.


In R:
spdep::moran.test(x, spdep::nb2listw(nb))

Related: Spatial autocorrelation, Neighbors and spatial weights · Lessons: 17


Multicollinearity
Regression
Strong correlation among predictors, which makes their separate effects hard to estimate.
The model can estimate the combined effect but not how to split it, so individual coefficients get large standard errors and maximum likelihood may fail to converge. Lagged temperatures and multiple pollutants are typical examples. Hierarchical priors and penalization stabilize them.

Formal definition. Measured by the variance inflation factor, \(VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\), where \(R_j^2\) comes from regressing \(x_j\) on the other predictors. \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) is multiplied by \(VIF_j\).

Related: Hierarchical (multilevel) model, Penalized spline, Distributed lag model (DLM) · Lessons: 7, 16, 24


Multiple testing (multiplicity)
Testing and intervals
Running many tests raises the chance that at least one is falsely significant.
With 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, the chance of at least one false positive is 64%. Corrections such as Bonferroni (α/m per test) control this at the cost of power. Hierarchical models offer a Bayesian alternative by shrinking noisy estimates.

Formal definition. Family-wise error rate for \(m\) independent tests: \(1 - (1 - \alpha)^m\). Bonferroni rejects when \(p_j < \alpha / m\).

Related: Type I error, Hierarchical (multilevel) model · Lessons: 6, 24

title: Glossary and symbols
text:
N

Natural cubic spline
Nonlinear effects
A cubic spline constrained to be linear beyond the outer knots, which tames behavior at the extremes.

In R:
splines::ns(temp, df = 4)

Related: Spline, Knot · Lessons: 11, 15, 16


Negative binomial distribution
Distributions
A distribution for overdispersed counts: like Poisson, but with variance larger than the mean.
It can be seen as a Poisson whose rate itself varies at random (a gamma mixture). The emergency visits in Example A were simulated this way.

Formal definition. \(E[Y] = \mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\phi\), where \(\phi > 0\) is the shape (size) parameter. As \(\phi \to \infty\) it becomes Poisson.


In R:
MASS::glm.nb(visits ~ temp, data = d)

Related: Overdispersion, Poisson distribution, Quasi-Poisson model (dispersion parameter) · Lessons: 3, 8


Negative predictive value (NPV)
Diagnostic accuracy
The probability that someone with a negative test does not have the condition.

Formal definition. \[NPV = P(D^- \mid T^-) = \frac{Sp(1 - p)}{Sp(1 - p) + (1 - Se)\,p}\]

Related: Positive predictive value (PPV), Specificity · Lessons: 2


Neighbors and spatial weights
Spatial
A definition of which areas count as neighbors, written as a matrix W.

Formal definition. \(w_{ij} = 1\) if areas \(i\) and \(j\) share a border (queen: share a border or corner), else 0; often row-standardized.


In R:
spdep::poly2nb(districts_sf, queen = TRUE)

Related: Moran’s I, Conditional autoregressive (CAR) model · Lessons: 17, 25


Nested models
Model building
Two models where one is a special case of the other, obtained by fixing some parameters.
A model without temperature is nested in one with temperature (β = 0). A linear and a threshold model are not nested. Likelihood ratio tests need nested models; AIC and Bayes factors don’t.
Related: Likelihood ratio test (LRT), Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayes factor · Lessons: 10, 23


Nominal variable
Describing data
A categorical variable whose categories have no natural order, such as district.
Nominal variables are summarized with counts and proportions. In regression they enter as a set of indicator (dummy) variables compared with a reference category, or, when there are many categories, as random effects.

Formal definition. A variable taking values in a finite set \(\{c_1, \dots, c_K\}\) with no ordering. Only equality (\(=\), \(\neq\)) is meaningful.

Related: Ordinal variable, Binary variable · Lessons: 1


Non-centered parameterization (funnel)
Hierarchical models
Rewriting group effects as standardized effects times τ, which removes a funnel-shaped geometry that makes sampling fail.

Formal definition. Centered: \(\theta_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \tau^2)\). Non-centered: \(z_j \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,1)\), \(\theta_j = \mu + \tau z_j\).

Related: Divergent transition, Hierarchical (multilevel) model · Lessons: 24


Non-collapsibility
Causal inference
A property of the odds ratio: the marginal OR differs from the conditional OR even when there is no confounding.
Adding a strong predictor of the outcome that is unrelated to the exposure moves the OR away from 1. So a change in the OR after adjustment is not proof of confounding.

Formal definition. Because \(\mathrm{logit}\,E_Z[\mathrm{expit}(\alpha + \beta x + \gamma z)] \ne \alpha' + \beta x\), the marginal log-OR differs from \(\beta\) when \(\gamma \ne 0\).

Related: Odds ratio (OR), Marginal and conditional effects · Lessons: 12


Non-differential misclassification
Measurement error
Misclassification whose rates are the same in all groups being compared.
For a binary exposure with independent errors, it biases associations toward the null. For an exposure with three or more categories, or with correlated errors, it can bias away from the null.
Related: Differential misclassification, Misclassification · Lessons: 13


Normal distribution
Distributions
The symmetric bell-shaped distribution described by its mean and standard deviation.
It arises as the distribution of averages (central limit theorem), and underlies linear regression, many confidence intervals, and many priors. About 95% of its mass lies within 1.96 SDs of the mean.

Formal definition. \[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\] written \(X \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)\).


In R:
dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

Related: Central limit theorem (CLT), Standard error (SE), Linear regression · Lessons: 3, 4


Null hypothesis (H0)
Testing and intervals
The hypothesis a test tries to find evidence against, usually “no effect”.
A frequentist test can reject the null or fail to reject it, never accept it. “No evidence of an effect” is not “evidence of no effect”; for that, use an equivalence test.

Formal definition. A statement about a parameter, such as \(H_0: \beta = 0\), against an alternative \(H_1: \beta \neq 0\).
