title: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction
text:
9.1 Confounding and stratification
Children in high-traffic districts have, on average, lower socio-economic position (SES), and lower SES independently raises asthma risk. SES is a confounder: it opens a non-causal route between NO₂ and asthma. Stratification compares children within groups of similar SES; regression does the same thing more smoothly. This section uses the true NO₂ exposure, available only in the simulation, so that confounding is the only source of bias.


  SES strata
  




Further reading: Lash et al. (2021) on confounding and its control; Hernán and Robins (2020) define confounding through causal structures; Keiding and Clayton (2014) trace stratification and standardization to regression.
crumbs: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction

title: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction
section: 9.2 Using a DAG to choose what to adjust for
text:
9.2 Using a DAG to choose what to adjust for
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) draws the assumed causal relations. Each arrow means “directly causes”. Non-causal paths from NO₂ to asthma that start with an arrow into NO₂ are backdoor paths; they create confounding unless blocked. A path is blocked by adjusting for a non-collider on it. A collider (a node where two arrows meet) blocks a path on its own, and adjusting for it opens the path. Click variables to adjust for them, and watch the paths and the estimated odds ratio.


  
  Click a variable to adjust for it (filled = adjusted). The arrows match the model that generated the data. "Clinic visit" is a variable created for this demonstration.
  Use a minimal adjustment setAdjust for nothingAdjust for everything






AStandard notation

\[\mathrm{SES} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{asthma}, \quad \mathrm{SES} \rightarrow \mathrm{asthma}\] \[\text{adjustment set } Z: \ Y^{x} \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Z\]

The backdoor criterion: \(Z\) blocks every backdoor path from \(X\) to \(Y\), and contains no descendant of \(X\).




BModel list and R

dag <- dagitty::dagitty("dag {
  SES -> NO2; SES -> Asthma; SES -> Smoke
  Smoke -> Asthma; Green -> NO2; Green -> Asthma
  Traffic -> NO2; Sex -> Asthma; NO2 -> Asthma
  Asthma -> Wheeze; NO2 -> Clinic; Asthma -> Clinic
}")
dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, "NO2", "Asthma")



CHow it’s reported

The adjustment set was chosen from a DAG of assumed causal relations (Supplementary Figure S1): SES and green space. Parental smoking, sex and district traffic were not required for confounding control.








WarningCommon pitfall



Adjusting for every available variable. Adjusting for a collider (here, clinic attendance) or for a consequence of the outcome (the wheeze questionnaire) creates bias. Adjusting for a variable that only affects the exposure (traffic) costs precision for no gain.








NoteR code (optional): adjustment sets and adjusted estimates






dag <- dagitty::dagitty("dag {
  SES -> NO2; SES -> Asthma; SES -> Smoke; Smoke -> Asthma
  Green -> NO2; Green -> Asthma; Traffic -> NO2; Sex -> Asthma
  NO2 -> Asthma; Asthma -> Wheeze; NO2 -> Clinic; Asthma -> Clinic
}")
dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "NO2", outcome = "Asthma")

#> { Green, SES }

fit <- glm(asthma ~ I(no2_true / 10) + ses + green, family = binomial, data = cohort)
exp(coef(fit)[2])   # close to the true OR of 1.15

#> I(no2_true/10) 
#>       1.148946






Further reading: Greenland et al. (1999) introduced causal diagrams to epidemiology; Hernán et al. (2004) explain selection bias as collider bias; Textor et al. (2016) describe the dagitty software; Westreich and Greenland (2013) on why adjustment variables’ coefficients need not be interpretable.

title: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction
section: 9.3 Effect modification: compare effects, not p-values
text:
9.3 Effect modification: compare effects, not p-values
Heat raises emergency visits more among older people. When an effect differs across levels of another variable, that variable is an effect modifier. The right test is of the difference between the effects. A common error is to report “significant in one group, not in the other” as evidence of a difference: the non-significant group may just have less data. Choose a district and compare the age groups.


  District
  Compare 65+ with0–1415–64
  






AStandard notation

\[\log\mu_{tk} = \alpha_k + \beta_k (T_t - 22) + \gamma^\top \mathrm{dow}_t\] \[z = \frac{\hat\beta_{65+} - \hat\beta_{0\text{–}14}}{\sqrt{SE_{65+}^2 + SE_{0\text{–}14}^2}}\]



BModel list and R

summer <- visits |>
  filter(month(date) %in% 6:8,
         district == "Lakeside")
glm(visits ~ age_group * I(temp - 22) + dow,
    family = quasipoisson, data = summer)



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Matthews and Altman (1996) “compare effect sizes, not P values”; Knol and VanderWeele (2012) recommend how to present effect modification; VanderWeele and Knol (2014) give a full tutorial.
crumbs: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction

title: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction
section: 9.4 Interaction on the additive and multiplicative scales
text:
9.4 Interaction on the additive and multiplicative scales
Is the harm of high NO₂ larger among children whose parents smoke? The answer depends on the scale. On the multiplicative scale (ratios), the question is whether the NO₂ risk ratio differs between groups. On the additive scale (differences), it is whether NO₂ causes more extra cases in one group. The additive scale tells you where reducing exposure prevents the most cases.


  Second factora parent smokeslow SES (bottom third)boy
  






AStandard notation

\[RERI = RR_{11} - RR_{10} - RR_{01} + 1\] \[\text{multiplicative: } \frac{RR_{11}}{RR_{10}\,RR_{01}}\]

\(RR_{ab}\): risk with NO₂ level \(a\) and factor level \(b\), relative to neither.




BModel list and R

cohort |>
  mutate(no2 = no2_true >= 30) |>
  group_by(no2, parent_smoke) |>
  summarise(risk = mean(asthma))



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



Hypotheses such as “heat harms the elderly more than children, and children not at all” can be stated as constraints on several parameters and compared directly with Bayes factors. Lesson 23 does exactly this for age-group heat effects.



Further reading: VanderWeele and Knol (2014) on additive and multiplicative interaction and the RERI; Knol and VanderWeele (2012) on reporting both scales; Lash et al. (2021) on effect-measure modification.

title: Lesson 9 · Confounding, effect modification and interaction
text:
Key takeaways

A confounder opens a non-causal path between exposure and outcome. Stratification or regression on it closes that path.
What to adjust for is decided by causal assumptions, best made explicit in a DAG.
Adjusting for a collider, a mediator, or a consequence of the outcome introduces bias. Adjusting for a cause of the exposure only (an instrument) costs precision.
Effect modification is assessed by estimating the difference between effects, not by comparing p-values.
Interaction depends on the scale. Report effects on both additive and multiplicative scales.

title: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs
text:
About 3 hours Before this: Lessons 8 and 10 Threads: shrinkage
Throughout this lesson the outcome is daily city-wide emergency visits, modeled by quasi-Poisson regression adjusted for season and day of week. The exposure is the average temperature over the same day and the three before it. (Lesson 16 models the lags properly.)
crumbs: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs

title: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs
text:
11.1 Categories: the step function
The simplest way to allow a nonlinear effect is to cut temperature into categories and estimate a rate ratio for each, relative to a reference category. The result is a step function: flat within each category, with jumps at arbitrary cut-points. Days just either side of a cut-point are treated as completely different; days at opposite ends of a category as identical.


  Number of categories
  Cut-points atquantiles (equal numbers of days)equal-width temperature bands
  




Further reading: Bennette and Vickers (2012) argue against quantile categories in epidemiology; Royston et al. (2006) on the costs of dichotomizing; Greenland (1995) on alternatives to categorical dose–response analysis.
crumbs: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs

title: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs
text:
11.2 Polynomials and their wild tails
Adding T², T³ and so on lets the curve bend smoothly. But polynomials are global: every coefficient affects the whole curve, so data in the middle of the range dictate behavior at the extremes, where data are sparse. High-degree polynomials swing wildly at the edges, exactly where heat and cold effects matter most.


  Polynomial degree
  




Further reading: Harrell (2015) on why polynomials and categories are inferior to splines; Fox (2016) on polynomial regression; Greenland (1995) on modeling dose–response trends.
crumbs: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs

title: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs
text:
11.3 Regression splines: local flexibility
A spline joins polynomial pieces smoothly at points called knots. A natural (restricted) cubic spline is also forced to be straight beyond the outer knots, which tames the tails. It enters the model as a set of basis functions: new columns in the design matrix, each multiplied by its own coefficient. The fitted curve is their weighted sum. More knots mean more flexibility.


  Knots
  
  






AStandard notation

\[\log \mu_t = \alpha + f(T_t) + \gamma^\top z_t, \qquad f(T) = \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \beta_k B_k(T)\] \[RR(T) = \exp\{f(T) - f(T_{\text{ref}})\}\]

\(B_k\) are the spline basis functions; \(z_t\) the season and day-of-week terms; \(T_{\text{ref}}\) the reference temperature.




BModel list and R

visits[t] ~ quasipoisson(mu[t])
log(mu[t]) = a + f(temp[t]) + season + dow

fit <- glm(visits ~ splines::ns(temp03, df = 3) +
             sin(2*pi*doy/365.25) +
             cos(2*pi*doy/365.25) + dow,
           family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): a spline exposure–response curve relative to its minimum






city_daily <- visits |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(visits = sum(visits), temp = first(temp_city), dow = first(dow), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(doy = yday(date),
         temp03 = (temp + lag(temp, 1) + lag(temp, 2) + lag(temp, 3)) / 4) |>
  filter(!is.na(temp03))

fit <- glm(visits ~ splines::ns(temp03, df = 3) + sin(2*pi*doy/365.25) + cos(2*pi*doy/365.25) + dow,
           family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)

grid <- tibble(temp03 = seq(-5, 30, by = 0.5), doy = 180, dow = factor("Wed", levels = levels(city_daily$dow)))
grid$logmu <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)
grid |> mutate(rr = exp(logmu - min(logmu))) |>
  ggplot(aes(temp03, rr)) + geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Mean temperature, lags 0-3 (°C)", y = "Rate ratio vs minimum")












Further reading: Perperoglou et al. (2019) compare spline procedures in R; Harrell (2015) on restricted cubic splines and knot placement; Wood (2017) on regression splines and their basis functions.
crumbs: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs

title: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs
section: 11.4 Penalized splines and generalized additive models
text:
11.4 Penalized splines and generalized additive models
Choosing the number of knots is a choice of flexibility, and choosing it by looking at the results is data dredging. A penalized spline uses many knots, then restrains wiggliness with a penalty. A small penalty gives a wiggly curve; a large one shrinks it toward a straight line. The effective degrees of freedom measure the flexibility actually used. In a GAM, the penalty is estimated from the data. Move the penalty and watch the curve and the AIC.


  Penalty (log scale)
  Choose the penalty by AIC
  









WarningCommon pitfall



Trying several numbers of knots, or several sets of cut-points, and reporting the one that gives the most striking result. Fix the flexibility in advance, or let a penalty chosen by a criterion such as AIC or cross-validation decide.








TipBayesian preview



A penalty that shrinks spline coefficients toward a straight line is mathematically the same as a prior that says “the curve is probably smooth”. In a Bayesian model the penalty becomes a random-walk or smoothing prior whose strength is learned from the data. Lesson 25 uses this for the temperature curve and the time trend.



Further reading: Eilers and Marx (1996) introduced P-splines; Wood (2017) is the standard book on GAMs and penalty selection; Perperoglou et al. (2019) on penalized splines in R.

title: Lesson 11 · Nonlinear effects: categories, polynomials, splines and GAMs
text:
Key takeaways

Categorizing a continuous exposure gives a step function that depends on arbitrary cut-points and wastes information.
Polynomials are global and unstable at the extremes of the data.
Regression splines are flexible locally and well behaved; natural (restricted) cubic splines are linear beyond the outer knots.
Penalized splines let the data choose the flexibility, measured by effective degrees of freedom.
Present nonlinear effects as rate ratios relative to a stated reference, with confidence bands.

title: Lesson 13 · Measurement error and misclassification
text:
13.1 Classical and Berkson error
Classical error adds noise to the true value: a noisy monitor, a crude exposure model. It flattens exposure–response slopes toward zero, which is called regression dilution. Berkson error goes the other way: everyone is assigned a group value, such as their district’s average, and the true values scatter around it. It barely biases a linear slope, but it widens the confidence interval. Change the error type and size, and compare the estimate with the truth.


  Exposure used in the analysistrue NO₂ plus classical errordistrict average of true NO₂ (Berkson)the cohort's modeled NO₂
  Error standard deviation (µg/m³)
  
  expected under classical errorthis analysistruth






AStandard notation

\[\text{classical: } W = X + U, \quad U \perp X\] \[\text{Berkson: } X = W + U, \quad U \perp W\] \[\hat\beta_W \approx \lambda\,\beta, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2_{X \mid Z}}{\sigma^2_{X \mid Z} + \sigma^2_U}\]

\(X\) = true exposure, \(W\) = measured, \(Z\) = covariates; \(\lambda\) is the reliability ratio (attenuation factor).




BModel list and R

# classical error attenuates
glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green,
    family = binomial, data = cohort)
# true exposure (simulation only)
glm(asthma ~ I(no2_true / 10) + ses + green,
    family = binomial, data = cohort)



CHow it’s reported





Further reading: Carroll et al. (2006) is the standard text; Armstrong (1998) explains classical and Berkson error for environmental exposures; Zeger et al. (2000) apply these ideas to air pollution studies.

title: Lesson 13 · Measurement error and misclassification
text:
13.2 Validation data and regression calibration
To correct for classical error you need to know how big it is. A validation study measures the exposure better in a subsample: here, 280 children wore personal NO₂ monitors. Regression calibration uses the validation data to predict each child’s true exposure from the error-prone one, then fits the outcome model with the predicted exposure. Its key ingredient is the calibration slope, which is usually below 1.


  Children in the validation study
  Draw a different validation subsample
  






AStandard notation

\[E[X \mid W, Z] = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 W + \alpha_2^\top Z \quad \text{(validation data)}\] \[\mathrm{logit}\,P(Y = 1) = \beta_0 + \beta\,\widehat{E}[X \mid W, Z] + \gamma^\top Z\]



BModel list and R

val <- cohort |> filter(validation)
cal <- lm(no2_personal ~ no2_modeled + ses + green,
          data = val)
cohort$no2_cal <- predict(cal, newdata = cohort)
glm(asthma ~ I(no2_cal / 10) + ses + green,
    family = binomial, data = cohort)



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): regression calibration with a bootstrap interval






rc_or <- function(d) {
  cal <- lm(no2_personal ~ no2_modeled + ses + green, data = filter(d, validation))
  d$no2_cal <- predict(cal, newdata = d)
  exp(coef(glm(asthma ~ I(no2_cal / 10) + ses + green, family = binomial, data = d))[2])
}
naive <- exp(coef(glm(asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green, family = binomial, data = cohort))[2])
c(naive = unname(naive), calibrated = unname(rc_or(cohort)))

#>      naive calibrated 
#>   1.049147   1.088262

set.seed(13)
boot <- map_dbl(1:200, \(b) rc_or(slice_sample(cohort, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))

#>      2.5%     97.5% 
#> 0.9029321 1.3283195






Further reading: Rosner et al. (1990) developed regression calibration for logistic regression; Keogh et al. (2020) give practical guidance on validation studies and simple corrections; Shaw et al. (2020) cover more complex methods.

text:
13.3 SIMEX: correcting by adding more error
If the error variance is known, simulation extrapolation (SIMEX) estimates what the result would be with no error by first making the error worse. Add extra noise of increasing size, refit, and watch the estimate fall. Then extrapolate the trend back to the point where the total error would be zero.


  Assumed error SD of modeled NO₂
  Run SIMEX
  




Further reading: Cook and Stefanski (1994) introduced SIMEX; Carroll et al. (2006) explain its extrapolation step; Shaw et al. (2020) compare SIMEX with other corrections.

title: Lesson 13 · Measurement error and misclassification
text:
13.4 Misclassification of binary variables
For binary variables, measurement error is misclassification, described by sensitivity and specificity. Suppose the analysis used the wheeze questionnaire instead of a clinical diagnosis of asthma. If the questionnaire errs equally in high- and low-NO₂ children (non-differential), the odds ratio is usually biased toward 1. If parents of highly exposed children report wheeze more readily (differential), the bias can go either way. Knowing or assuming sensitivity and specificity, you can correct the counts.


  Sensitivity, low-NO₂ children
  Sensitivity, high-NO₂ children
  Specificity (both groups)
  Make it non-differential
  






AStandard notation

\[E[a^*] = Se\cdot a + (1 - Sp)(n - a)\] \[\hat a = \frac{a^* - (1 - Sp)\, n}{Se + Sp - 1}\]

\(a^*\) = observed positives in a group of size \(n\); \(\hat a\) = corrected number of true cases.




BModel list and R

correct <- function(pos, n, se, sp)
  (pos - (1 - sp) * n) / (se + sp - 1)
# or a probabilistic bias analysis:
# episensr::probsens(...)



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Assuming that non-differential error always biases toward the null, so a non-null result must be “conservative”. That holds only on average and for binary exposures with independent errors. For exposures with three or more categories, for errors that are correlated with errors in confounders, or in any single study by chance, the estimate can be pushed away from the null.








TipBayesian preview



A Bayesian measurement-error model treats each child’s true exposure as an unknown parameter, informed by the modeled value, the validation data and its relation to the outcome, all at once. Uncertainty about the error is carried into the final interval automatically. Lesson 24 builds this as a hierarchical model.



Further reading: Jurek et al. (2005) on why non-differential misclassification need not bias a single study toward the null; Fox et al. (2021) on simple and probabilistic bias analysis for misclassification; Keogh et al. (2020) on misclassification in observational epidemiology.

15.1 What’s in a daily series?
A daily count of emergency visits mixes several patterns: a slow long-term trend, an annual seasonal cycle, a weekly day-of-week cycle, holidays, and day-to-day noise that may contain the effects of temperature and pollution we want to study. A regression model separates them. Switch each component on to see its contribution.

   trend  season  day of week
  Show yearall five years20202021202220232024
  
  
  


Further reading: Bhaskaran et al. (2013) is a widely used tutorial on time-series regression in environmental epidemiology; Peng and Dominici (2008) cover the methods with R examples; Armstrong (2006) discusses temperature–mortality models.

title: Lesson 15 · Time-series regression for health data
section: 15.2 How much to control for time?
text:
15.2 How much to control for time?
A spline of time with a few degrees of freedom per year removes the seasons and trends. Too few, and seasonal confounding leaks into the pollution estimate. Too many, and the spline starts to absorb the short-term variation that carries the information about pollution. The usual approach is to examine how the estimate changes across a range, and to choose the flexibility in advance. Here the question is the effect of PM2.5 (average of the same and previous day) on daily visits, adjusted for temperature and day of week.


  Degrees of freedom per year for time
   adjust for temperature
  






AStandard notation

\[Y_t \sim \text{quasi-Poisson}(\mu_t)\] \[\log\mu_t = \alpha + \beta\,\overline{PM}_{t,t-1} + s(t; \text{df}) + f(T_t) + \gamma^\top \mathrm{dow}_t\]

\(s(t; \text{df})\) = natural spline of time; \(f\) = spline of temperature.




BModel list and R

fit <- glm(visits ~ pm01 +
             splines::ns(t, df = 7 * 5) +
             splines::ns(temp, df = 3) + dow,
           family = quasipoisson,
           data = city_daily)








WarningCommon pitfall



Choosing the degrees of freedom for time by looking at which value gives the most striking (or the most significant) pollution estimate. Fix the choice in advance from the literature, typically 4 to 8 per year, and report the sensitivity analysis.








NoteR code (optional): sensitivity of the PM2.5 estimate to the time spline






city_daily <- visits |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(visits = sum(visits), temp = first(temp_city), pm25 = first(pm25),
            dow = first(dow), holiday = first(holiday), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(t = row_number(), pm01 = (pm25 + lag(pm25)) / 2 / 10) |>
  filter(!is.na(pm01))

fit_df <- function(df_per_year) {
  f <- glm(visits ~ pm01 + splines::ns(t, df = df_per_year * 5) + splines::ns(temp, df = 3) + dow,
           family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily)
  b <- coef(f)["pm01"]; s <- sqrt(vcov(f)["pm01", "pm01"])
  tibble(df_per_year, rr = exp(b), low = exp(b - 1.96 * s), high = exp(b + 1.96 * s),
         dispersion = summary(f)$dispersion)
}
map(c(2, 4, 7, 10), fit_df) |> bind_rows()

#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   df_per_year    rr   low  high dispersion
#>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1           2  1.08  1.07  1.08       2.03
#> 2           4  1.06  1.05  1.07       1.71
#> 3           7  1.06  1.06  1.07       1.66
#> 4          10  1.07  1.06  1.07       1.63






Further reading: Peng et al. (2006) study how the choice of time adjustment affects pollution estimates; Bhaskaran et al. (2013) give practical guidance on choosing degrees of freedom; Peng and Dominici (2008) on sensitivity analyses.

15.3 Residual autocorrelation and dispersion
After the time spline, residuals should look like noise. If today’s residual still predicts tomorrow’s, standard errors are too small. The autocorrelation function shows this, lag by lag. With the model from 15.2, see how the residual autocorrelation and dispersion change with the degrees of freedom.





Further reading: Bhaskaran et al. (2013) on residual checks in time-series studies; Peng and Dominici (2008) on autocorrelation and overdispersion; Fox (2016) on GLM residuals.

title: Lesson 15 · Time-series regression for health data
text:
15.4 The time-stratified case-crossover design
A case-crossover study compares each case’s exposure on the day of the event with the same person’s exposure on nearby control days. In the time-stratified version, control days are the other days on the same weekday in the same month and year. Each stratum then acts as its own comparison, so season, trend and day of week are controlled by design. Analyzed with a conditional Poisson model, it is equivalent to a time-series model with an indicator for every stratum.







AStandard notation

\[\log\mu_t = \alpha_{s(t)} + \beta\,\overline{PM}_{t,t-1} + f(T_t)\] \[L_c(\beta) = \prod_s \prod_{t \in s}\left(\frac{e^{\beta x_t}}{\sum_{t' \in s} e^{\beta x_{t'}}}\right)^{y_t}\]

\(s(t)\) = stratum (year × month × weekday). Conditioning on each stratum’s total removes \(\alpha_s\).




BModel list and R

city_daily <- city_daily |>
  mutate(stratum = interaction(year(date),
                               month(date), dow))
glm(visits ~ pm01 + splines::ns(temp, df = 3) +
      stratum, family = quasipoisson,
    data = city_daily)
# or gnm::gnm(..., eliminate = stratum)



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



In a Bayesian time-series model, the smooth function of time can be given a random-walk prior, which says that each week’s level is close to the previous week’s. Its smoothness is then estimated from the data rather than chosen as a number of degrees of freedom. Lesson 25 uses this for the trend.



Further reading: Maclure (1991) introduced the case-crossover design; Janes et al. (2005) show why time-stratified referents avoid bias; Armstrong et al. (2014) explain the conditional Poisson model and its equivalence with case-crossover analysis.

title: Lesson 17 · Spatial data and spatial autocorrelation
section: 17.1 Standardized morbidity ratios and the small-numbers problem
text:
17.1 Standardized morbidity ratios and the small-numbers problem
An SMR compares the number of visits a district actually had with the number expected if each age group had the city-wide rate (indirect standardization, Lesson 1). An SMR of 1.2 means 20% more visits than expected for its age structure. Shorten the period, and the counts, and watch how noisy the map becomes. The funnel plot shows why: the range of SMRs expected by chance alone is much wider for small expected counts.


  Period2020–2024 (five years)2023July 20231–7 July 20233 July 2023 (one day)
  Age groupall ages0–1465+
  






AStandard notation

\[E_j = \sum_k r_k\, PT_{jk}, \qquad SMR_j = \frac{O_j}{E_j}\] \[O_j \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(E_j\,\theta_j) \ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{SE}(SMR_j) \approx \frac{\sqrt{O_j}}{E_j}\]

\(r_k\) = city-wide rate in age group \(k\); \(\theta_j\) = the district’s true relative risk.




BModel list and R

rates <- visits |> group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(r = sum(visits) / sum(population))
visits |> left_join(rates, by = "age_group") |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(O = sum(visits),
            E = sum(r * population),
            smr = O / E)



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Ranking areas by their raw SMRs, or labeling the most extreme as “hot spots”, without considering their expected counts. On a funnel plot, a small district outside the 95% limits may still be within the range expected by chance once you allow for 12 comparisons.



Further reading: Spiegelhalter (2005) introduced funnel plots for comparing institutions; Elliott and Wartenberg (2004) review spatial epidemiology; Waller and Gotway (2004) on SMRs and indirect standardization for small areas.

title: Lesson 17 · Spatial data and spatial autocorrelation
text:
17.2 Spatial autocorrelation and Moran’s I
Neighboring districts share air, housing and populations, so their values tend to be similar. Moran’s I measures this: it is positive when neighbors resemble each other, near zero when they don’t. Its significance is tested by permutation: shuffle the values among districts many times, and see how often chance alone gives an I as large as the observed one.


  VariabledeprivationtrafficSMR, all ages, five yearsSMR after adjusting for deprivationrandom noise
  






AStandard notation

\[I = \frac{n}{\sum_{ij} w_{ij}}\;\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar x)(x_j - \bar x)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}\]

\(w_{ij} = 1\) if districts \(i\) and \(j\) are neighbors (here: share a border or a corner), row-standardized. Under no autocorrelation, \(E[I] = -1/(n-1)\).




BModel list and R

nb <- lapply(strsplit(districts$neighbors, " "),
             as.integer)
class(nb) <- "nb"
lw <- spdep::nb2listw(nb, style = "W")
spdep::moran.mc(districts$deprivation, lw,
                nsim = 999)








NoteR code (optional): SMRs and Moran’s I with spdep






rates <- visits |> group_by(age_group) |> summarise(r = sum(visits) / sum(population), .groups = "drop")
smr <- visits |>
  left_join(rates, by = "age_group") |>
  group_by(district_id) |>
  summarise(O = sum(visits), E = sum(r * population), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(smr = O / E) |>
  arrange(district_id)

nb <- lapply(strsplit(districts$neighbors, " "), as.integer)
class(nb) <- "nb"
lw <- spdep::nb2listw(nb, style = "W")
spdep::moran.mc(smr$smr, lw, nsim = 999)

#> 
#>  Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I
#> 
#> data:  smr$smr 
#> weights: lw  
#> number of simulations + 1: 1000 
#> 
#> statistic = 0.095085, observed rank = 902, p-value = 0.098
#> alternative hypothesis: greater

spdep::moran.mc(districts$deprivation, lw, nsim = 999)

#> 
#>  Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I
#> 
#> data:  districts$deprivation 
#> weights: lw  
#> number of simulations + 1: 1000 
#> 
#> statistic = -0.01325, observed rank = 726, p-value = 0.274
#> alternative hypothesis: greater






Further reading: Moran (1950) introduced the statistic; Bivand et al. (2013) cover neighbor structures and Moran’s I in R; Waller and Gotway (2004) on testing spatial autocorrelation in health data.

section: 17.3 Ecological associations and the ecological fallacy
text:
17.3 Ecological associations and the ecological fallacy
With district-level data only, the association between NO₂ and asthma has to be estimated from 12 points: district asthma risk against district mean NO₂. This ecological association need not equal the individual-level one. District-level confounding, by deprivation for example, can distort it, and with few areas it is very imprecise. Concluding from an area-level association to individuals is the ecological fallacy.


   adjust the ecological model for district mean SES
  




Further reading: Robinson (1950) first described the ecological fallacy; Greenland and Morgenstern (1989) explain ecological bias, confounding and effect modification; Elliott and Wartenberg (2004) on when ecological designs are informative.

title: Lesson 17 · Spatial data and spatial autocorrelation
text:
17.4 Smoothing small-area estimates
With small counts, each district’s SMR is noisy. An empirical Bayes estimate pulls each SMR toward the city-wide value by an amount that depends on its own precision: districts with few expected visits move a lot, large ones hardly at all. Here the five-year SMRs serve as the “truth” against which one week’s raw and smoothed SMRs are judged.


  Short periodJuly 20231–7 July 20233 July 2023
  Age group0–1465+all ages
  






AStandard notation

\[\hat\theta_j^{\text{EB}} = w_j\, SMR_j + (1 - w_j)\,\hat\mu, \qquad w_j = \frac{\hat\sigma^2_\theta}{\hat\sigma^2_\theta + \hat\mu / E_j}\]

\(\hat\mu\) and \(\hat\sigma^2_\theta\): mean and between-district variance of the true relative risks, estimated by the method of moments (Marshall, 1991).




BModel list and R

mu   <- sum(O) / sum(E)
s2   <- sum(E * (smr - mu)^2) / sum(E) -
        mu / mean(E)
s2   <- max(s2, 0)
w    <- s2 / (s2 + mu / E)
smr_eb <- w * smr + (1 - w) * mu



CHow it’s reported










TipBayesian preview



Empirical Bayes shrinks every district toward one city-wide value. A full Bayesian disease-mapping model (BYM2, Lesson 25) shrinks each district partly toward the city mean and partly toward its neighbors, with the balance between the two estimated from the data, and with uncertainty for every district.



Further reading: Clayton and Kaldor (1987) introduced empirical Bayes estimates of relative risk for disease mapping; Marshall (1991) gave the method-of-moments estimator used here; Efron and Morris (1977) explain why shrinkage improves many estimates at once.

title: Lesson 19 · Bayesian thinking: from Bayes’ rule to a model equation
text:
19.1 Bayes’ rule for a risk
Lesson 2 used Bayes’ rule to update the probability of asthma after a test result. Here it updates beliefs about a parameter: the risk of asthma by age 8. Start from a prior distribution, observe some children, and get a posterior. With a beta prior and binomial data, the posterior is also a beta distribution, so the update is simple arithmetic: add the cases and non-cases to the prior’s counts.


  Children observed
  Prior mean of the risk
  Prior strength (equivalent children)
  
  priorlikelihood (scaled)posterior






AStandard notation

\[\pi \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b), \qquad d \mid \pi \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, \pi)\] \[\pi \mid d \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + d,\ b + n - d)\]

\(a + b\) is the prior’s strength in “equivalent children”; \(a/(a+b)\) its mean.




BModel list and R

d ~ binomial(n, p)
p ~ beta(a, b)

a_post <- a + d; b_post <- b + n - d
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), a_post, b_post)



CHow it’s reported










NoteR code (optional): conjugate updating and a grid posterior






set.seed(19)
smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 50)
d <- sum(smp$asthma); n <- nrow(smp)
a <- 2; b <- 18                      # prior mean 10%, worth 20 children

# exact conjugate answer
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), a + d, b + n - d)

#> [1] 0.1156036 0.1971324 0.3006042

# the same posterior by brute force on a grid: prior x likelihood, rescaled
grid <- tibble(p = seq(0.001, 0.999, by = 0.001)) |>
  mutate(prior = dbeta(p, a, b), lik = dbinom(d, n, p),
         post = prior * lik / sum(prior * lik))
grid |> summarise(mean = sum(p * post),
                  low = p[which(cumsum(post) >= 0.025)[1]],
                  high = p[which(cumsum(post) >= 0.975)[1]])

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>    mean   low  high
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   0.2 0.116 0.301






Further reading: Greenland (2006) introduces Bayesian methods for epidemiologists; Gelman et al. (2013) chapter-length treatments of conjugate models; Spiegelhalter et al. (2004) on priors as “equivalent data” in health research.

title: Lesson 19 · Bayesian thinking: from Bayes’ rule to a model equation
section: 19.2 The model equation builds the likelihood
text:
19.2 The model equation builds the likelihood
Now a regression. On summer days (June to August), how do emergency visits by Lakeside’s older residents depend on temperature? The model equation gives each day’s expected count from two parameters, α and β; the Poisson distribution turns that expectation into a probability for the count that actually happened. Multiply over days and you have the likelihood of that pair (α, β). Do it for every pair and you get a likelihood map. Click anywhere on it.


  Summer days of data
  
  Across: β, the effect per °C. Up: the expected visits at 20°C, eα. Darker = more likely. The ring marks your choice.






AStandard notation

\[y_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_t), \qquad \log\mu_t = \alpha + \beta\,(T_t - 20)\] \[L(\alpha, \beta) = \prod_t \frac{\mu_t^{y_t} e^{-\mu_t}}{y_t!}\]



BModel list and R

visits[t] ~ poisson(mu[t])
log(mu[t]) = a + b * (temp[t] - 20)

loglik <- function(a, b)
  sum(dpois(d$visits,
            exp(a + b * (d$temp - 20)), log = TRUE))



Further reading: McElreath (2020) builds Bayesian models from the model equation upward; Pawitan (2001) on the likelihood as the shared ingredient; Held and Sabanés Bové (2020) on likelihood and Bayesian inference together.
crumbs: Lesson 19 · Bayesian thinking: from Bayes' rule to a model equation

title: Lesson 19 · Bayesian thinking: from Bayes’ rule to a model equation
section: 19.3 Multiply by the prior: the posterior map
text:
19.3 Multiply by the prior: the posterior map
The prior is another map over the same (α, β) plane: how plausible each version of the equation seemed before the data. The posterior is the two maps multiplied point by point, then rescaled. That is all “likelihood × prior” means. Try a narrow prior centered on zero (a skeptic), then a narrow prior centered on a large effect, then add more days.



  Prior mean of β (% per °C)
  Prior SD of β (% per °C)




Prior
× Likelihood
= Posterior






AStandard notation

\[p(\alpha, \beta \mid y) \propto p(y \mid \alpha, \beta)\; p(\alpha)\, p(\beta)\] \[\beta \sim \mathrm{Normal}(m, s^2), \qquad \alpha \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\log 8, 1)\]



BModel list and R

visits[t] ~ poisson(mu[t])
log(mu[t]) = a + b * (temp[t] - 20)
a ~ normal(log(8), 1)
b ~ normal(0, 0.03)

brms::brm(visits ~ I(temp - 20), family = poisson,
  prior = c(prior(normal(2.08, 1), class = Intercept),
            prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = b)),
  data = d)

19.4 Back to the equation: posterior draws
Draw points from the posterior map, as MCMC does in practice, and plug each one into the model equation. Each draw gives one curve. The bundle of curves is the Bayesian answer, expressed in the language of the model. Any question, such as the effect per °C, the expected visits on a 30°C day, or the probability that heat increases visits, is answered by computing it on every draw.

Draw again





AStandard notation

\[(\alpha^{(s)}, \beta^{(s)}) \sim p(\alpha, \beta \mid y), \quad s = 1, \dots, S\] \[\text{95\% credible interval for } \beta: \ \big[\beta_{(0.025)},\ \beta_{(0.975)}\big]\]



BModel list and R

draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit)
quantile(draws$b_ItempM20, c(.025, .5, .975))
mean(draws$b_ItempM20 > 0)         # P(heat harmful)
mean(exp(draws$b_Intercept +
         10 * draws$b_ItempM20))    # visits at 30°C



CHow it’s reported










WarningCommon pitfall



Thinking a Bayesian model has a different equation from the frequentist one. The model equation and the likelihood are the same; the prior is the only new ingredient. With plenty of data and a weakly informative prior, the posterior median and credible interval closely match the maximum likelihood estimate and the confidence interval. The interpretation is what differs.



Further reading: Gelman et al. (2013) on summarizing posterior simulations; Kruschke (2015) on credible intervals and posterior probabilities; Bland and Altman (1998) on Bayesian and frequentist interpretations side by side.

title: Lesson 19 · Bayesian thinking: from Bayes’ rule to a model equation
text:
Key takeaways

Bayes’ rule for a parameter: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. With a beta prior and binomial data, the update just adds counts.
The model equation, plus a distribution for the outcome, builds the likelihood. Prior and posterior are distributions over the equation’s parameters.
Multiplying prior and likelihood point by point gives the posterior; it lies between them, closer to whichever is more precise.
Posterior draws, plugged into the model equation, give a bundle of curves; any question is answered by computing on the draws.
A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% posterior probability, given the model, prior and data.

21.1 The Metropolis algorithm
The Metropolis algorithm is a random walk with one rule. From the current value, propose a jump of random size. If the posterior is higher there, move. If it’s lower, move only with probability equal to the ratio of the two heights; otherwise stay put. Over many steps, the chain visits each value in proportion to its posterior density. Here it samples the risk of asthma from 30 cases in 200 children, with a Beta(2, 18) prior, so the exact answer is known for comparison.


  Step size (SD of proposals)
  Starting value
  1 step100 steps2,000 stepsReset
  
  






AStandard notation

\[\theta^* \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\theta^{(s)}, \sigma^2_{\text{step}})\] \[\theta^{(s+1)} = \begin{cases} \theta^* & \text{with probability } \min\!\left(1, \dfrac{p(\theta^* \mid y)}{p(\theta^{(s)} \mid y)}\right) \\ \theta^{(s)} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]



BModel list and R

log_post <- function(p) if (p <= 0 || p >= 1) -Inf else
  dbinom(30, 200, p, log = TRUE) + dbeta(p, 2, 18, log = TRUE)
theta <- numeric(5000); theta[1] <- 0.6
for (s in 2:5000) {
  prop <- rnorm(1, theta[s - 1], 0.03)
  accept <- log(runif(1)) < log_post(prop) - log_post(theta[s - 1])
  theta[s] <- if (accept) prop else theta[s - 1]
}








NoteR code (optional): a Metropolis sampler checked against the exact posterior






set.seed(21)
log_post <- function(p) if (p <= 0 || p >= 1) -Inf else
  dbinom(30, 200, p, log = TRUE) + dbeta(p, 2, 18, log = TRUE)
theta <- numeric(5000); theta[1] <- 0.6
for (s in 2:5000) {
  prop <- rnorm(1, theta[s - 1], 0.03)
  theta[s] <- if (log(runif(1)) < log_post(prop) - log_post(theta[s - 1])) prop else theta[s - 1]
}
kept <- theta[-(1:500)]                       # discard warm-up
rbind(metropolis = quantile(kept, c(.025, .5, .975)),
      exact      = qbeta(c(.025, .5, .975), 2 + 30, 18 + 170))

#>                 2.5%       50%     97.5%
#> metropolis 0.1019709 0.1433161 0.1947115
#> exact      0.1021411 0.1443794 0.1948669

mean(diff(theta) != 0)                        # acceptance rate

#> [1] 0.6325265






Further reading: Metropolis et al. (1953) introduced the algorithm; Hastings (1970) generalized it; Gelman et al. (2013) on Markov chain simulation for posteriors.

21.2 Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the shape of the posterior
With two or more correlated parameters, a random walk struggles: proposals that move along the narrow ridge of the posterior are rare. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), the method behind Stan and brms, uses the slope of the log posterior to glide along it, like a frictionless puck on a curved surface, making long moves that are still likely to be accepted. Compare the two samplers on the Lakeside heat model of Lesson 19, with temperature centered at 20°C or left uncentered.


  Random-walk MetropolisHamiltonian Monte Carlo
  Temperature centered at 20°CTemperature uncentered (°C)
  Run 300 iterationsReset
  






AStandard notation

\[H(\theta, r) = -\log p(\theta \mid y) + \tfrac12 r^\top r\] \[r \leftarrow r + \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla_\theta \log p(\theta \mid y), \quad \theta \leftarrow \theta + \epsilon\, r, \quad r \leftarrow r + \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla_\theta \log p(\theta \mid y)\]

The last line is one leapfrog step, repeated L times per iteration; \(r\) is a random momentum.




BModel list and R

# brms / Stan use an adaptive HMC (NUTS):
fit <- brms::brm(visits ~ I(temp - 20),
                 family = poisson, data = d,
                 chains = 4, iter = 2000,
                 warmup = 1000)



Further reading: Betancourt (2017) is an accessible introduction to HMC; Hoffman and Gelman (2014) introduced the No-U-Turn sampler used by Stan; Carpenter et al. (2017) describe Stan.

21.3 Has it converged? Trace plots, R-hat and effective sample size
A sampler gives no warning on its own when it fails. Standard practice runs several chains from different starting points and checks that they agree. Trace plots should look like overlapping, well-mixed “hairy caterpillars”. R-hat compares variation between and within chains; values above 1.01 signal trouble. The effective sample size (ESS) says how many independent draws the correlated chain is worth.


  HealthyToo shortStep size too smallUncentered, random walk
  
  chain 1chain 2chain 3chain 4






AStandard notation

\[\hat R = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{N-1}{N}W + \frac{1}{N}B}{W}}, \qquad \text{ESS} = \frac{M N}{1 + 2\sum_{k \ge 1}\rho_k}\]

\(W\): average within-chain variance; \(B\): between-chain variance (× \(N\)); \(M\) chains of length \(N\) (after splitting each in half); \(\rho_k\): autocorrelation at lag \(k\).




BModel list and R

summary(fit)            # Rhat, Bulk_ESS, Tail_ESS
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(fit)
posterior::summarise_draws(fit)








WarningCommon pitfall



Reporting results from a model with R-hat above 1.01, low effective sample sizes, or divergent-transition warnings. These aren’t cosmetic: they mean the draws may not represent the posterior. Fix the model (reparameterize, center predictors, use better priors) before interpreting it.








TipBayesian preview



The hardest posterior shape for samplers is the funnel that appears in hierarchical models when the group-level SD is small: a narrow neck where the step size must be tiny, opening into a wide mouth. Stan flags it with divergent transitions. Lesson 24 shows the funnel and the standard cure, the non-centered parameterization.



Further reading: Gelman and Rubin (1992) introduced R-hat; Vehtari et al. (2021) give the improved rank-normalized version used by Stan today; Gabry et al. (2019) on diagnostic plots in the Bayesian workflow.

text:
Key takeaways

Grids are infeasible beyond a few parameters; MCMC samples the posterior instead.
Metropolis accepts uphill moves always and downhill moves sometimes. Step sizes too small or too large both make it inefficient.
HMC uses the posterior’s gradient to make long, well-aimed moves; Stan’s NUTS tunes it automatically.
Centering predictors reduces posterior correlation and helps every sampler.
Run several chains; check trace plots, R-hat (≤ 1.01) and effective sample size before interpreting results.
